course.title: UX and Human–Computer Interaction
course.description: How people see, remember and decide at a screen, and how to find out whether a design works for them. Covers research methods, usability heuristics, interaction design and accessibility to WCAG 2.2.
course.audience: A capable adult who uses software every day and has never studied why some interfaces work and others fail. They know basic proportions and percentages and have met the idea of a sample. No design or coding experience is needed; two lessons read short HTML snippets.

paragraphs: Two greys, #767676 and #777777, look identical on a white page, yet text in the first meets the web's accessibility guidelines and text in the second does not. A menu of fifteen items takes only a little longer to choose from than a menu of seven, and a button against the very edge of the screen is easier to hit with a mouse than a much larger one floating in the middle. Each of these is a measured fact about people using screens, and human–computer interaction is the field that gathers such facts, from the way the eye groups what it sees to how much a person can keep in mind while they work.

Facts of this kind change how a design question is settled. Where a team might otherwise argue about whether a layout feels cluttered or a label seems clear, you can work out how hard a target is to reach, watch five people attempt a task and record what goes wrong, test whether the gap between two versions is larger than chance would produce, or calculate whether a colour pair can be read by someone with low vision. User experience design is the practice of applying these findings to one product and the people who use it, so that a design can be checked before it is built and again after it ships.
outcomes: You'll be able to explain why a screen is read the way it is, using grouping, attention and memory limits.
You'll be able to calculate pointing difficulty with Fitts's law and choice time with Hick's law, and say what each does not tell you.
You'll be able to choose a research method (interview, survey, card sort, usability test, A/B test) for a given question, and spot a leading question.
You'll be able to judge an interface against Nielsen's ten heuristics and rate the severity of what you find.
You'll be able to check a colour pair, a touch target and a form against the relevant WCAG 2.2 success criteria.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Psychology: How Minds Work, Probability and Statistics.

modules.title: How people see, remember and act
modules.description: The limits of perception, memory and movement that every layout works within.

modules.title: Finding out what users need
modules.description: Interviews, surveys, card sorts, usability tests and experiments, and what each can and cannot show.

modules.title: Judging and shaping interactions
modules.description: Heuristics, expert inspection, severity, and the details of forms, errors and feedback.

modules.title: Accessibility
modules.description: WCAG 2.2 as a working checklist: contrast, keyboard, structure and target size.

concepts.title: Gestalt grouping
concepts.summary: Viewers perceive nearby, similar, enclosed or aligned elements as belonging together before they read any of them.

concepts.title: Visual hierarchy
concepts.summary: Size, contrast and position set the order in which a viewer's attention visits elements on a screen.

concepts.title: Working memory
concepts.summary: The small store that holds the items a person is using right now, estimated at roughly four chunks in recent work.

concepts.title: Chunking
concepts.summary: Grouping items into meaningful units so that more information fits in the same number of slots.

concepts.title: Recognition versus recall
concepts.summary: Picking an item from a visible set takes less memory than producing it from nothing.

concepts.title: Fitts's law
concepts.summary: Time to reach a target grows with the index of difficulty ID = log2(D/W + 1), where D is distance to the target and W its width along the line of motion (Shannon formulation).

concepts.title: Hick's law
concepts.summary: For n equally likely choices the decision time grows as b·log2(n + 1).

concepts.title: Response-time limits
concepts.summary: About 0.1 s feels instant, 1 s keeps the flow of thought, and 10 s is the limit of attention on a task.

concepts.title: Mental model
concepts.summary: A person's working picture of how a system behaves, which may differ from how it is built.

concepts.title: Signifier
concepts.summary: A perceivable cue that shows where and how an action can be taken.

concepts.title: Gulf of execution
concepts.summary: The gap between what a user wants to do and the actions the system makes available and visible.

concepts.title: Gulf of evaluation
concepts.summary: The gap between the system's state and the user's ability to perceive and interpret it.

concepts.title: Leading question
concepts.summary: A question whose wording suggests the answer wanted.

concepts.title: Margin of error
concepts.summary: For a proportion p from n independent responses, 95% margin = 1.96·sqrt(p(1−p)/n).

concepts.title: Say versus do
concepts.summary: What people report about their behaviour often differs from what they do.

concepts.title: Card sort
concepts.summary: Participants group content items into categories, showing the structure they expect.

concepts.title: Tree test
concepts.summary: Participants find items in a text-only hierarchy, measuring whether the structure and labels work.

concepts.title: Breadth and depth
concepts.summary: A hierarchy with b choices per level and d levels can reach b^d items.

concepts.title: Think-aloud protocol
concepts.summary: Participants speak their thoughts while they work on a task, revealing what they notice and expect.

concepts.title: Problem discovery model
concepts.summary: With a per-user detection rate L, n users find a proportion 1 − (1 − L)^n of the problems; Nielsen and Landauer's average L was about 0.31.

concepts.title: System Usability Scale
concepts.summary: Ten five-point items scored (odd items: response − 1; even items: 5 − response), summed and multiplied by 2.5, range 0 to 100.

concepts.title: A/B test
concepts.summary: Randomly assign users to two versions and compare a metric.

concepts.title: Two-proportion z
concepts.summary: z = (p2 − p1) / sqrt(p1(1−p1)/n1 + p2(1−p2)/n2); at the 95% level |z| must exceed 1.96.

concepts.title: The why gap
concepts.summary: Analytics show what users did, and give no reason.

concepts.title: Usability heuristic
concepts.summary: A broad rule of thumb for judging an interface, derived from patterns in found problems.

concepts.title: Nielsen's ten heuristics
concepts.summary: Visibility of system status; match between system and real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency of use; aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors; help and documentation.

concepts.title: Heuristic evaluation
concepts.summary: Several evaluators independently inspect an interface against heuristics and then merge their findings.

concepts.title: Severity rating
concepts.summary: A 0–4 scale, from not a problem to usability catastrophe, based on frequency, impact and persistence.

concepts.title: Cognitive walkthrough
concepts.summary: An evaluator steps through a task asking, at each action, whether the user will try it, notice it, connect it to the goal and see progress.

concepts.title: Error prevention
concepts.summary: Design that makes the error impossible or unlikely, such as constraints, defaults and reversible actions.

concepts.title: Anatomy of an error message
concepts.summary: A good error message says what happened, why, and what to do next, in the user's words, next to the field.

concepts.title: Undo over confirmation
concepts.summary: Allowing a reversal is usually better than asking 'Are you sure?', which users answer by habit.

concepts.title: POUR
concepts.summary: WCAG organises requirements under four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

concepts.title: Conformance levels
concepts.summary: Success criteria are levelled A, AA and AAA; AA is the usual legal and policy target.

concepts.title: Contrast ratio
concepts.summary: (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the lighter colour's relative luminance; AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and for key interface components (1.4.3, 1.4.11).

concepts.title: Keyboard operability
concepts.summary: Every function works from a keyboard (2.1.1), focus is visible (2.4.7) and not hidden behind other content (2.4.11).

concepts.title: Semantic markup
concepts.summary: Native elements such as button, label, and headings give assistive technology a name, role and state without extra code (4.1.2).

concepts.title: Target size minimum
concepts.summary: Pointer targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have enough spacing (2.5.8, AA, new in WCAG 2.2).

lessons.title: How the eye groups a screen

reveal.text: Three groups of two: the 8 px gaps join dots and the 40 px gaps separate the pairs. The next screen names the rule.

lead.text: The figure shows the same six dots twice. In the first view they are evenly spaced and the eye sees a single row, and in the second the gaps alternate between 8 px and 40 px and the same dots become three pairs. Grouping by nearness is called **proximity**, and it is a comparison between gaps, so the 8 px that joins two dots in one layout would separate them in another where every gap was 2 px.

afterFigure.text: Max Wertheimer described grouping by proximity in a paper of 1923, as part of the Gestalt school of psychology, which holds that a viewer perceives organised wholes before the parts that make them up. The consequence for a form is the one in the opening figure: a label must be nearer to its own field than to any other element, so that the gap, which is seen first, agrees with the words, which are read second.

diagram.caption: The same six dots with different gaps. The 8 px gaps join neighbours and the 40 px gaps separate the pairs.

lead.text: Proximity is one cue among several. In the figure every dot is the same distance from its neighbours, so distance says nothing, yet each view still shows three pairs. Elements that look alike are read as members of one set, a cue called **similarity**, and elements that sit inside one outline or on one background panel are read as a single unit, a cue called **common region**.

afterFigure.text: Common region is the strongest of the three, because an outline is an explicit boundary, and it can override proximity: two buttons 8 px apart in separate panels read as separate, while two buttons 40 px apart on one panel read as together. Similarity needs more care, because it asserts likeness: a viewer who sees two things in the same colour takes them to be alike in function.

reveal.text: The panel is an outline in everything but name. It groups the three controls although the gaps around them are the same as everywhere else.

lead.text: Two further cues act along lines. Elements whose left edges fall on the same vertical line are read as a **column**, and the eye follows that edge down the page, which is why a ragged left edge makes a list look as though it has no structure. A row of icons at one height with one spacing is read as a row for a related reason: the eye tends to carry on in the direction it is already moving, a cue called **continuity**, and an element that leaves the line is read as a break in the sequence.

afterFigure.text: Alignment is the cheapest grouping cue, because it costs no extra space or ink, and designers use it for most of a page and keep boxes and colours for the few places that need a stronger cue.

steps.headline: Diagnose the sign-up form and repair it using gaps alone.

workedSteps.text: Measure the two gaps around the label Password: it is 8 px below the Email field and 24 px above the Password field.
Proximity compares the gaps and the smaller one wins, so the label joins the Email field, which is the wrong one.
The label is therefore nearer to the wrong field than to its own, by the difference between the two gaps.
Change the gaps so that the label sits 4 px above its own field and 24 px below the previous field.
The smaller gap now belongs to the field the label names, so the grouping agrees with the words, and no new element has been added.

lead.text: Grouping decides what belongs together; **visual hierarchy** decides what is looked at first. Three properties set it: the size of an element, its contrast with the background, and its position, since in languages read from left to right the eye starts at the top left of a page.
A quick test is to squint at a page, or blur it, until the words can no longer be read. What remains is the pattern of dark and coloured masses, which is the order in which a viewer will visit them.

afterFigure.text: If the button the page exists for disappears when you squint, or a decorative banner is the darkest thing in the blur, the page is ranking the wrong things first.

reveal.text: That ranking is the page's visual hierarchy. It can be changed without moving anything, by making an element larger, darker or more different from its surroundings.

lead.text: When two cues give different groupings, the viewer hesitates. In the figure the gaps make three pairs, but in the second view colour joins dots across the wide gaps, and the eye cannot settle on either reading. The same happens with a reused style. On a page where links are blue and underlined, the viewer learns after a few examples that blue underline means a link, and a phrase of ordinary text that is styled the same way is then clicked, and found to do nothing.

afterFigure.text: Colour is therefore part of the meaning of a page and not decoration. Each time a colour or a shape is used, it tells the viewer that this element belongs with the others that wear it, so a style should be reserved for the one kind of thing it names. When a grouping looks wrong, the cause is usually two cues pulling against each other, and the repair is to change the weaker one so that they agree.

lessons.orientation: How proximity, similarity, common region and alignment decide which elements a viewer reads as one group, and how hierarchy orders them.
lessons.reviewLabel: How the eye groups a screen
lessons.nextAction: Count how many items working memory can hold, and design so that people need to remember fewer.

blocks.text: In a sign-up form, the label Password sits 8 px below the Email field and 24 px above the Password field it names. Before reading a word, almost everyone attaches the label to the Email field, because the smaller gap tells the eye that two things belong together, and moving the label to 4 px above its own field and 24 px below the previous one repairs the form without adding a line, a box or a word.

A layout is read twice, first as shapes in a fraction of a second and then as words, and the first reading decides what the words are taken to mean. The eye follows a small number of rules in making that first reading.

diagram.alt: A sign-up form with an Email field above a Password label and field. In the first view the label is 8 px below the Email field and 24 px above its own field; in the second it is 24 px below the Email field and 4 px above its own field.

recap.keyIdea: Viewers read nearness, shared appearance, shared enclosure and shared edges as grouping before they read any word, and size, contrast and position set the order in which the groups are visited.

blocks.text: You saw that a label nearer to the wrong field is read as belonging to it, and that proximity is a comparison between gaps, so it can be repaired by moving a label alone. Similarity and common region group at any distance, with common region the stronger, and alignment groups at no cost. When two cues disagree the viewer hesitates, so a colour or a shape should be used for one kind of thing only.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from what the eye sees to what the mind can hold, and shows how many items a person can keep in mind at once.

lessons.title: What memory can hold

reveal.text: Only a handful. The next screen gives the limits that studies have found and the way grouping lets the same small store carry more.

lead.text: The store used for the items a person is working with right now is called **working memory**, and its capacity is small. George Miller's paper of 1956, "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two", is the source of the figure many people quote, but Miller was describing the span for items, and he noted that the unit could be stretched by recoding. Nelson Cowan reviewed the evidence in 2001 and argued that the limit is nearer four. Neither number is a design rule to be applied exactly, and the safe reading is that the store is very small.

What fills it is not the number of digits or words but the number of units. A **chunk** is a group of items that a person already treats as one thing, such as a familiar phone-number group or a well-known word, and **chunking** is the grouping of items into chunks.

afterFigure.text: Chunking depends on what the reader already knows. To someone who knows the letters, FBI is one chunk, and to someone who does not, it is three, so a designer chunks a string by splitting it where readers expect the splits to fall.

lead.text: Grouping the eleven digits turned them into four units, each of which the reader treats as one thing.

reveal.text: That unit is what the rest of the lesson counts. A screen should be judged by how many chunks it asks a person to carry, not by how many characters it contains.
The options are all on screen, so nothing has to be remembered. The next screen explains why that matters.

lead.text: There are two ways of getting an item out of memory. In **recall** the person produces it with no cue on the screen, as when they type a command at a blank prompt, and in **recognition** the person picks it from options that are shown, as when they choose Copy from a menu. Recognition is easier because the options act as cues, and nothing has to be held in working memory until it is needed.
A long menu is a search problem, because the cost is scanning, and the memory problem appears only when a user must remember the name of an option that is not on screen.

afterFigure.text: Show any code on the same page where it is needed, keep related choices together, and split long strings into groups, since each of these removes something from working memory.

steps.headline: Count how much grouping saves on the string 07700900123.

workedSteps.text: Without grouping, every digit is its own item, so the string asks for eleven items.
Grouped as 077 009 001 23, each group is read as one unit, which gives four chunks.
The saving is how much less the person has to hold at once.

lead.text: Every task asks for some memory and attention, and **cognitive load** is the name for the total. Part of it comes from the task itself: an accountant adding a column of figures must hold the running total whatever the screen looks like. Another part is added by the layout, as when two related fields are on different pages or a code must be remembered across a page change, and this part is called **extraneous load**, because the design could remove it.

Design aims at extraneous load, since it can be reduced and the load of the task cannot. A checkout that says "enter the code from the previous page" puts a six-digit code in memory, while one that shows the code beside the box removes it entirely.

reveal.text: The user must carry two chunks across the page change. Putting the code on the page where it is typed removes that load, which is the cheapest improvement available.
Five chunks is above the roughly four that working memory holds, so the sensible design is to keep the key visible beside the box, or to let the user copy and paste it.

lessons.orientation: Working memory is small, chunking makes it go further, and recognition spares it altogether.

What has changed is the number of separate things you have to hold at once, and the mind can keep only a limited number of them in an active store while it works.

intro.whyItMatters: Memory limits turn a sensible-looking screen into one that causes errors.

recap.keyIdea: Working memory holds only a few chunks, so a screen should group items into chunks and show options and state instead of asking people to remember them.

blocks.text: You counted units and not characters, and found that eleven digits can cost four chunks while the same digits unbroken cost eleven. Recognition keeps the options on screen, so it asks for far less than recall, and extraneous load such as a code carried across pages is the part of the load a design can remove.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from memory to movement and choice, with two formulas that predict how long it takes to point at a target and to pick one option from many.

lessons.title: Distance, size and the number of choices

lead.text: In Fitts's experiments, the time to reach a target depended on two things: the distance to it and its width.

reveal.text: The two changes help by the same amount. The next screen shows why.

lead.text: Paul Fitts's tapping experiments of 1954 asked people to move between two targets as fast as they could, and found that movement was quicker for wider and nearer targets. In human-computer interaction it is written as the **index of difficulty**, ID = log2(D/W + 1), measured in bits, where D is the distance to the target and W is its width along the line of motion.

With D = 7 cm and W = 1 cm the ratio is 7, and log2(7 + 1) = log2(8) = 3 bits. Doubling W to 2 cm gives a ratio of 3.5 and an ID of log2(4.5), about 2.17 bits. Because D and W enter only as a ratio, halving the distance would have given the same 3.5, which is why neither change beats the other.

afterFigure.text: The index does not give a time directly. The movement time is modelled as a straight-line function of it, MT = a + b × ID, where a and b are constants found by measuring the particular device and user. The formula therefore ranks designs reliably, and predicts an absolute time only after its constants have been measured.

workedSteps.text: The distance is 14 cm and the width is 2 cm, so D/W is 7.
Add 1 and take the base-2 logarithm, since 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
Now keep the distance at 14 cm and widen the target to 7 cm.

reveal.text: D/W is 3 and 3 + 1 = 4, a power of 2, which is why the logarithm comes out whole.

lead.text: The width in Fitts's law is measured along the line of motion, and a mouse pointer cannot travel past the edge of the screen. A button at the top edge, such as the menu bar on many desktops, can therefore be reached by pushing the pointer upward as far as it will go, with no need to stop precisely, and a corner target gains the same advantage in two directions. In the model, the width W of such a target is effectively unlimited, and its index of difficulty falls to a small value.

Three design rules follow. Make the primary button large, since W sits in the denominator. Put controls that are used together near each other, since D falls. Place a destructive button away from the ones used often, since a high ID makes an accidental hit less likely, which is the one case where difficulty is a feature.

reveal.text: At the edge the pointer cannot overshoot, so the width along the movement counts as unlimited. Moved 60 px away, the button is only as wide as it is drawn, and the index of difficulty rises.

lead.text: William Hick in 1952 and Ray Hyman in 1953 found that the time to choose among n equally likely options grows as log2(n + 1), multiplied by a constant b found by measurement. A menu of 31 items gives log2(32) = 5, and a menu of 63 gives log2(64) = 6. Doubling the list therefore adds one unit of b, and does not double the time.

This is why Hick's law is not the same as saying that fewer items are always better. The time grows slowly, so a well-organised list of 15 can beat a menu of three levels, where each level costs its own decision and its own page. The law also assumes that the options are equally likely and that the user does not already know where the item is, and it ignores labels and grouping, which affect real choices a great deal.

lead.text: Robert Miller's study of 1968 and later work by Nielsen give three limits. About **0.1 s** feels instant, so that the user sees the response as caused directly by the action. About **1 s** keeps the flow of thought uninterrupted, although the user notices the delay. About **10 s** is the limit of attention on a task, and beyond it people turn to something else.

A response slower than the limit calls for feedback: a pressed state within 0.1 s, a progress indicator for anything slower than a second, and a percentage or a time estimate for delays near ten seconds.

reveal.text: Each doubling adds one unit. A designer who halves the number of items per screen gains one unit, but adds a level of navigation that costs its own decision.

recap.keyIdea: The time to point depends on the ratio of distance to width through ID = log2(D/W + 1), the time to choose grows as log2(n + 1), and neither formula includes familiarity, labels or grouping.

blocks.text: You calculated the index of difficulty for several targets, and saw that edges and corners behave as if they were unlimited in size. For choice, doubling a list adds one unit and not twice the time, which makes organisation a better lever than cutting items. Response-time limits of 0.1 s, 1 s and 10 s then say how long a system may take before the user needs feedback.

lead.text: A person's working picture of how a system behaves is their **mental model**, and it is built from experience, guesses and whatever the screen shows. It may differ from how the system is actually built, and still be useful, as when someone treats a thermostat as a tap that makes the room warmer faster the higher it is set. The designer has a model too, the one the system was built to follow, and the two people never meet.
What connects them is the **system image**, which is everything the user can see and do: the labels, the layout, the feedback, the manual.

afterFigure.text: Because the system image is the only channel, a user whose picture is wrong has usually been given a poor image. The design must therefore show what can be done and what has happened.

lead.text: James Gibson coined the word **affordance** in 1979 for what an environment allows an animal to do, and Don Norman brought it into design in 1988. A door affords pushing, and a chair affords sitting, whether or not anyone can tell. The word is often misused for any visible hint on a screen, which is a different thing: a hint that is perceivable and says where and how to act is a **signifier**, a term Norman introduced in the revised edition of The Design of Everyday Things in 2013.

A flat plate on a door is a signifier for pushing, because there is nothing to grip, and a handle is a signifier for pulling. A button's raised edge, a link's underline and a text field's box are signifiers on a screen. A signifier can be missing, as when an affordance exists and nothing shows it, and it can be wrong, as when a handle is fitted to a door that must be pushed.

reveal.text: The three short lines are a signifier. The card's ability to be dragged is the affordance.

lead.text: Norman describes using a system as a loop. The user forms a goal, plans an action and carries it out, the system changes, and the user perceives the new state, interprets it and compares it with the goal.

The **gulf of execution** is the gap between what the user wants to do and the actions the system makes available and visible. In the second view an icon-only toolbar has no labels, so the user who wants to export cannot tell which action is the right one. The **gulf of evaluation** is the gap between the system's state and the user's ability to perceive and interpret it. In the third view a thermostat shows only the target temperature, so the user has set it correctly and still cannot tell whether the heating is running.

afterFigure.text: Both gulfs are properties of the design, since each depends on what the system shows. When a user fails, the first question is which stage of the loop gave way, and the answer tells the designer where to repair.

reveal.text: The goal is clear and the command is hidden inside a menu the user never opens. That is a gap in execution, and a clearer label or a visible Crop button narrows it.
The user pressed Start correctly and still cannot tell what the machine is doing. That gap lies after the action, in reading the machine's state, so it is the gulf of evaluation.

lead.text: A design narrows the gulf of execution by making the available actions visible and by limiting the wrong ones. A **constraint** limits the options, as a plug that fits one way only, and a **mapping** is the relation between a control and its effect, which is natural when the layout of the controls copies the layout of the things they control, as on a stove whose four knobs sit in the same square as its four burners.

It narrows the gulf of evaluation with **feedback**, which is a visible, immediate report of what the system did, such as a button that changes as it is pressed and a message that says what was saved.

reveal.text: A door affords pushing, and the plate or handle is only the signifier that shows or contradicts it.
Locate the failure in the design and a repair follows, such as a label, a tooltip or a menu item where people look.

blocks.text: Many doors carry a small sign saying PUSH or PULL, fixed beside a handle or a plate that ought to have made the sign unnecessary. Most doors open in one of only two ways, so a sign of this kind is a written correction, added because enough people tried the wrong way for someone to notice, and the fault it corrects lies in what the door itself told them to do.

Failures like this are easy to blame on the person at the door, yet each can be traced to a particular part of the design: either the object did not show how to act on it, or it did not show what had happened once the person acted. Names for those two failures, and for the cues that prevent them, let you say of any screen where a user went wrong which part of the design let them down and what would repair it.

blocks.text: You compared a plate and a handle, and saw that an affordance is a property of the object while a signifier is something a designer adds or removes. The loop of goal, plan, act, perceive, interpret and compare locates a failure, and a gap in acting is a gulf of execution while a gap in reading is a gulf of evaluation. Constraints, mappings and feedback are the tools that narrow them.

lessons.title: Asking people: interviews and surveys

reveal.text: Only loosely. People describe what they did far more reliably than what they would use, and the next screen explains why.

lead.text: An **interview** is a conversation with one person at a time, in which the questions are open and the interviewer follows up, and it answers why. A **survey** gives the same closed questions to many people, with fixed choices or a scale, and it answers how many. Neither can show what people do, which is what observation is for.

The reason to prefer questions about past events is the **say-do gap**: what people report about their behaviour often differs from what they do, because they forget, tidy the story and say what they think is expected. People are also poor at designing solutions, so a question such as "Which features do you want?" returns guesses. A question such as "Tell me about the last time you tried to find a setting" returns an event.

reveal.text: The firmest question is the one about a past event. Wishes and forecasts are guesses, and a rating is an impression, so only the first returns what the person actually did.

lead.text: Three sources of bias account for most bad survey results. The first is wording: a **leading question** suggests the answer the asker wants, and a scale whose labels run only from "good" to "excellent" has the same effect. The second is **social desirability**, the tendency to answer as one thinks one should, which is why a question about a worthy habit overstates it. The third is **self-selection**, which arises when the people who answer are the ones who chose to, as with a pop-up that only the most annoyed or most pleased click.
Chance error averages out as responses accumulate, but bias pushes every response the same way, so a larger survey with a biased sample is simply a more precise wrong answer.

reveal.text: The gap between what is said and what is done is the say-do gap, and wanting to look good in front of the asker is a major cause.

lead.text: For a proportion p measured from n independent responses, the 95% **margin of error** is 1.96 × sqrt(p(1 − p)/n). With p = 0.5 and n = 100, the margin is 1.96 × sqrt(0.25/100) = 1.96 × 0.05 = 0.098, about 9.8 percentage points, so a result of 50% means that the true value probably lies between about 40% and 60%.

Because n sits under a square root, multiplying the sample by four halves the margin, from 9.8 points at n = 100 to 4.9 at n = 400, and a further factor of four brings it to about 2.5 at n = 1,600. Precision is therefore bought at an increasing price, and it covers only chance, since the formula assumes that the respondents were chosen at random.

steps.headline: Compute the 95% margin of error for p = 0.5 at n = 625 and then at n = 2,500.

workedSteps.text: At n = 625, p(1 − p) is 0.25 and dividing by 625 gives 0.0004, whose square root is 0.02.
Multiply by 1.96 to find the margin.
At n = 2,500, with p still 0.5, the square root works out as 0.01.

reveal.text: A proportion far from 0.5 has less spread, so the margin is smaller than at p = 0.5. The worst case is always p = 0.5.

lead.text: If the team needs to know why people struggle, an interview gives reasons and examples that a closed question would miss. If it needs to know how many people struggle, a survey gives a number with a margin, provided that the sample is not biased. If it needs to know what people actually do, it should watch them, because neither interview nor survey avoids the say-do gap.
A common order is to interview a few people to find out what matters, to survey many to measure it, and to observe a few to check that what people say agrees with what they do.

reveal.text: The cost grows with the square of the improvement. Four times the people halves the margin, which is why surveys are rarely sized for very small margins.

blocks.text: Here are two questions about a new search feature: "How much do you like the new search?" and "How did you find the last thing you looked for?" The first takes it for granted that the person likes the search and asks only for the amount, so it returns a number that looks like evidence, while the second asks about something that actually happened, and its answers will include the failures.

Asking people is the quickest way of learning what they think, and its errors are predictable. The wording of a question, the wish to make a good impression and the way respondents were chosen each push answers in one direction, while chance moves them both ways by an amount you can calculate.

lessons.title: Sorting content and testing where things are

reveal.text: More than a thousand: 12 × 12 × 12 is 1,728 items. The structure is explained in the later screens; first, how people expect content to be grouped.

lead.text: In a **card sort**, participants group cards, each naming a content item, into piles that make sense to them. In an **open card sort** they name the piles themselves, which generates ideas about structure and vocabulary. In a **closed card sort** the categories are given, and participants place the cards in them, which checks whether items fit categories that have already been chosen.

afterFigure.text: A card sort generates ideas. It does not test a navigation, because nothing is being searched for: the participants are free to sort, and the result still has to be turned into a structure and then checked by another method.

lead.text: Once a structure has been proposed, a **tree test** checks it. Participants see only a text hierarchy, with no page design, search or visual cues, and are given tasks such as "Find where to change your delivery address". They click down the tree until they decide they have found the answer, and the software records where each person ended up.

Two numbers summarise the result. The **success rate** is the share of participants who ended at the correct place, and **directness** is the share who went straight there without backing up. A high success rate with low directness means that people got there by wandering, and the structure or its labels are costing them effort.

afterFigure.text: Because the design is stripped away, a failure in a tree test points at the structure or the labels, and not at a button or a layout.

steps.headline: Read the results of a tree test in which 20 of 25 participants reached the right leaf.

workedSteps.text: The success rate is the participants who reached the leaf divided by those who tried.
A second task has 24 participants, and 18 of them reach the right leaf.
The second task has the lower rate, so it is the one to look at first.

reveal.text: The success rate is 80% and directness is 60%, so one participant in five failed and a further five found it only after wandering.

lead.text: The shape of a structure fixes how many items it can hold. If every level offers b choices and there are d levels, then the number of items reachable is b^d, since each choice opens another set of b. In the figure, four choices at each of three levels reach 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 items, and eight choices reach 8 × 8 × 8 = 512.

A designer can therefore trade breadth for depth. Neither is always better: because b^d grows quickly, a short hierarchy with clear labels reaches a large catalogue, and a deep menu with clear labels can beat a wide one with vague labels.

lead.text: A structure is read through its labels, so a hierarchy that groups correctly can still fail if its names are ones the users do not use. Internal words are the commonest cause: a company calls a section "Fulfilment" and the customer looks for "Delivery", or a bank's "Remittance" is a customer's "Send money". Card sorts give the users' words, and tree tests show where a label sent people astray.

A good label also tells people what is behind it before they click. Two labels that overlap, such as "Products" and "Solutions", send some people to the wrong branch, and show up in a tree test as a task with a low success rate and a few popular wrong answers.

reveal.text: Three levels reach only 1,000 items, and four reach 10,000, so four levels are the smallest number that covers 3,000.

The company's categories are accurate and still useless to the person who has to find something.
Card sorting and tree testing deal with that mismatch from two directions.

lessons.title: Watching people use it

reveal.text: The scenario with a goal and a deadline. The next screen explains why a task should not name the controls.

lead.text: In a moderated **usability test**, a participant works through tasks on the interface while a facilitator observes. The **think-aloud protocol** asks the participant to say what they are looking at, expecting and deciding as they go, which exposes the expectations that clicks alone would hide: a person who says "I would expect Delivery under Orders" has told the team what label and what place would have worked.

The task has to be a scenario, which gives a goal in the user's own terms, such as "Your parcel is arriving on a day you will be away; get it delivered a day later." A task that names the interface, such as "Click Orders and change the date", tests whether people can follow instructions and not whether they can find the way. The facilitator's role is to observe, and not to help or defend the design, and to probe afterwards by asking about what was seen.

afterFigure.text: Four measures come out of a test: whether the participant succeeded, how long it took, how many errors were made and how satisfied the participant felt.

reveal.text: The participant is narrating thoughts as they work, which gives the team their expectations at the moment they matter.

lead.text: Suppose each test user finds a proportion L of a product's problems, and that users find them independently. The chance that one particular problem is missed by a single user is 1 − L, the chance that n users all miss it is (1 − L)^n, and the share found is 1 − (1 − L)^n. This is the **problem discovery model** of Nielsen and Landauer.

The figure shows it with L = 0.31, where the first user finds 31%, five users find about 84% and eight find about 95%. Each added user gives less than the one before, because by then many of the problems have already been seen. The second view sets L at 0.15 for problems that are harder to stumble on, and shows that five users then find only about 56%.

afterFigure.text: Nielsen's article reports that five users find about 85% of the problems, and the exact value of the formula is 84%. The figure of L = 0.31 is an average, and it depends on the product and the tasks, so the formula is a planning guide and not a guarantee.

lead.text: After the tasks, a participant can fill in the **System Usability Scale**, which John Brooke published in 1996. It has ten statements, each answered from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The statements alternate between positive and negative, so the scoring differs for odd and even items.

For an odd item, the contribution is the response minus 1, and for an even item it is 5 minus the response, which puts every item on a scale of 0 to 4 with 4 the best. The ten contributions are added and the sum is multiplied by 2.5, giving a score from 0 to 100. In the figure, a participant who answered 4 on every odd item and 2 on every even item gets 3 from each item, a sum of 30, and a score of 75.

afterFigure.text: The score is not a percentage and not a share of anything. It is a position on a 0 to 100 scale, and the figure of about 68 is the commonly quoted average from many studies, so a score is read against that and against the same product's earlier score.

lead.text: The claim behind five users is that five per round find most of the problems for one group of users, and not that five is a whole study. The usual plan is to test with a few people, fix the problems found, and test again, because fixing the obvious ones lets the next round reach the less obvious ones, and because a different group of users, such as novices and experts, has different problems and needs its own round.

A test can be moderated, with a facilitator present, or unmoderated, run by software without one, and it can be in person or remote. Moderated tests allow probing and are best for finding why. Unmoderated tests are cheaper and reach many people, and they suit measuring success and time on clear tasks.

reveal.text: The gain per user falls quickly, so with L = 0.31 moving from 84% to 90% takes two more users and getting to 99% takes many more.

blocks.text: Jakob Nielsen and Thomas Landauer reported in 1993 that if each test user finds a proportion L of a product's usability problems, then n users find 1 − (1 − L)^n of them, and that L averaged about 0.31 across the projects they studied. With L = 0.31 and n = 5 the formula gives 1 − 0.69^5 = 0.8436, which is the origin of the widely repeated advice that five users are enough.

The advice is more careful than its slogan, and the arithmetic shows why: the first few users find many problems and later users mostly find the ones already seen, so a small test repeated after each round of fixes finds more than one large test run once.

A SUS sheet is scored by taking response − 1 for odd items and 5 − response for even ones, summing and multiplying by 2.5, and the result is read against an average near 68.

lessons.title: Experiments and analytics

reveal.text: The difference is not established by this test. The rest of the lesson shows how to check.

lead.text: In an **A/B test**, each visitor is assigned by chance to version A or version B, and a metric such as the share who sign up is compared. Random assignment is what makes the comparison fair, since it spreads every other difference between users, such as new against returning visitors or mobile against desktop, evenly across the two groups.

The metric is a proportion, and it varies from one group of users to the next even if the versions are identical, in the way a coin tossed a thousand times does not give exactly 500 heads. The question for the analysis is therefore how large the observed gap is compared with that natural variation.

reveal.text: That is not random assignment, since Monday visitors may differ from other visitors. Assigning each visitor by chance removes that problem.

lead.text: For two conversion rates p1 and p2 from n1 and n2 users, the variation of the difference is its standard error, sqrt(p1(1 − p1)/n1 + p2(1 − p2)/n2), and the statistic is **z** = (p2 − p1) divided by that standard error. A large z means the observed difference is large compared with the chance variation, and at the 95% level a difference is called significant when |z| exceeds 1.96.

For the opening example, with p1 = 0.040, p2 = 0.048 and n = 1,000 each, the standard error is sqrt(0.0000384 + 0.0000457) = sqrt(0.0000841), about 0.00917, so z = 0.008/0.00917, about 0.87. The figure draws the two rates as bell curves that show how much each could vary: at 1,000 users each they overlap heavily, and with ten times the users the curves narrow and the same difference gives z = 2.76.

afterFigure.text: The calculation uses the same difference throughout, and only the sample size changes, which is why a small test can miss a real difference and a very large one can find a trivial one.

diagram.alt: Two bell curves for the conversion rates of version A at 4.0% and version B at 4.8%. At 1,000 users each they overlap heavily and z is 0.87; at 4,000 each z is 1.74; at 10,000 each they separate and z is 2.76.
diagram.caption: The curves show how much each measured rate could vary by chance. More users make them narrower, so the same difference separates them.

steps.headline: Work out z for 5.0% against 6.0% with 2,000 users in each group.

workedSteps.text: Each rate has a variance p(1 − p)/n, and the two are added to give the variance of the difference.
The standard error is the square root of that sum.
The two rates, 5.0% and 6.0%, differ by 0.010.

reveal.text: The ratio exceeds 1.96, so this difference is significant, and it would be unlikely to arise by chance alone.

lead.text: A result with |z| above 1.96 is called **statistically significant** at the 95% level. It means that if the two versions were really the same, a difference this large would arise by chance less than one time in twenty. It does not prove that B is better by any amount, and it does not say that the difference matters, since a very large test can find a gain too small to be worth shipping.

The reverse also needs care. A result below 1.96, as in the opening example, does not show that the versions are equal. It shows that the test could not tell them apart, and a larger sample might still find a difference.

reveal.text: A z of 2.4 exceeds 1.96, so the difference is statistically significant, and the size of the gain still has to be judged on its own.

lead.text: The 95% rule assumes that the analysis is run once, on a sample size decided before the test began. A team that looks at the result each morning and stops at the first day on which |z| exceeds 1.96 gives chance many more chances to cross the line, and the share of false wins rises well above one in twenty. The remedy is to decide how many users to test, from the smallest difference worth detecting, and to read the result only when that number has been reached.

Analytics have a second limit, which is that they record what users did and not why. The funnel in the figure shows 1,000 users at step 1, 800 at step 2, 800 at step 3 and 320 who finish, so 480 of the 800 who reach step 3 leave, which is 60%. The counts locate the problem exactly and are silent about its cause, which is the **why gap**, and it is closed by watching or asking the people who left.

blocks.text: A team tests two versions of a sign-up page with 1,000 visitors each. Version A converts 4.0% of its visitors and version B converts 4.8%, so B looks 20% better and the obvious move is to ship it. Conversion rates move about from one group of visitors to the next even when nothing has changed, however, so the real question is whether a gap of 0.8 percentage points is larger than chance alone would produce with groups of this size.
An A/B test answers that with a short calculation, which divides the gap by the variation that chance would give and says whether the result holds at the 95% level.

blocks.text: You saw that 4.0% against 4.8% with 1,000 users each gives z = 0.87, which chance can easily produce, and that the same gap with ten times the users gives z = 2.76. lessons.title: Ten usability heuristics

reveal.text: The user is missing information about what the system is doing. The first heuristic is about exactly that.

lead.text: A **usability heuristic** is a broad rule of thumb, not a precise rule: it says what a good interface tends to do and leaves the evaluator to decide whether a given screen does it. Nielsen's list has ten, and the figure gives their names in order.

Because the rules are broad, a single problem can break more than one of them. A message that reads "Error 0x80070057" breaks the rule about plain language and the rule about explaining errors, and the evaluator should record the one that explains the most.

steps.headline: Status, language and control

lead.text: **Visibility of system status** asks the system to keep users informed about what is going on, with feedback in reasonable time. A twenty-second upload with no progress indicator breaks it. **Match between system and the real world** asks the system to speak the user's language, with words and concepts the user knows and not internal terms, and to follow real-world conventions. An error code such as 0x80070057 is the opposite of that.

**User control and freedom** acknowledges that users often choose an action by mistake and need a clearly marked emergency exit, such as undo, cancel and back. A record that is deleted immediately, with no way back, breaks it.

lead.text: **Consistency and standards** says that users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations or actions mean the same thing, and that conventions of the platform and of other products should be followed. **Error prevention** goes further than a good error message, since it removes the conditions in which an error is likely, or asks for confirmation before a costly action. **Recognition rather than recall**, met in the lesson on memory, asks that objects, actions and options be visible, so that users need not remember information from one part of the interface to another.
**Flexibility and efficiency of use** says that accelerators, unseen by the novice, may speed the interaction for the expert, such as keyboard shortcuts and the ability to tailor frequent actions.

reveal.text: The same action appears under two names and two styles. The heuristic about sameness is consistency and standards.
The code has to be carried in memory from one page to the next, which the lesson on working memory showed is costly. The heuristic is recognition rather than recall.

lead.text: **Aesthetic and minimalist design** says that screens should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed, since every extra unit of information competes with the relevant units and lowers their visibility. **Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors** says that error messages should be expressed in plain language, with no codes, say precisely what went wrong and suggest a solution. **Help and documentation** accepts that the best system needs no explanation, but says that where help is needed, it should be easy to search, focused on the user's task and short.

When a problem fits several heuristics, name the one that explains it best and say how it connects to the others. The code 0x80070057 is most fully explained by the error heuristic, since it describes what the message must contain, while its failure to speak the user's language is a secondary cause.

reveal.text: The message is in plain words, so the real-world language heuristic is met. It still gives no cause and no next step, and the heuristic about error messages is the one that asks for both.
Each extra option competes with the ones that matter. The heuristic about leaving out the unneeded is aesthetic and minimalist design.

lessons.orientation: The ten heuristics and how to assign a problem to the one that explains it best.
lessons.nextAction: Run a heuristic evaluation with several evaluators, and rate how serious each problem is.

blocks.text: Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich presented heuristic evaluation in 1990, and in 1994 Nielsen refined the list into the ten heuristics still used today, after analysing a large set of real usability problems to see which broad rules explained the most of them.

A heuristic is a broad rule of thumb for judging an interface, and the usefulness of the list is that it gives names to the problems that evaluators keep meeting. A reviewer who sees a spinner that runs for twenty seconds with no message can say which rule it breaks, and the name suggests the repair.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name Nielsen's ten heuristics and assign a described problem to the one it breaks.
intro.whyItMatters: Names for common problems let a team talk about them and point to a repair.

recap.keyIdea: Nielsen's ten heuristics are rules of thumb that name common usability problems, and a problem is assigned to the heuristic that explains it best.

blocks.text: You went through the ten in three groups: status, plain language and control; consistency, error prevention, recognition and efficiency; and minimalism, error messages and help. A single problem can break several of them, so the evaluator names the one that explains the most and notes the others.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows how evaluators use the heuristics in a structured inspection, how several of them combine their findings, and how to rate how serious each problem is.

lessons.title: Inspecting an interface and rating what you find

reveal.text: Somewhat less than 70%, about 57.8%, because some problems are found by both. The next screens give the method behind the number.

lead.text: In a **heuristic evaluation**, a small group of evaluators each go through the interface on their own, comparing it with the heuristics from the previous lesson and noting each problem with the screen it is on and the heuristic it breaks. Only afterwards do they meet to merge their lists into one.

The independent first pass is the heart of the method. If the evaluators agreed beforehand, or looked at one another's notes, they would tend to find the same things, and the lists would overlap more than they need to.

afterFigure.text: Inspection does not replace testing. It finds different problems, since experts miss some that real users hit and report others that no user would care about, so the two methods are used together.

reveal.text: That removes the independence the method depends on. The evaluators should each inspect alone first, so that their findings differ.

lead.text: If one evaluator finds 35% of the problems, the chance that a given problem is missed by that evaluator is 0.65. If evaluators work independently, the chance that n of them all miss it is 0.65^n, and the share found is 1 − 0.65^n. For two evaluators this is about 57.8%, for three about 72.5%, and for five about 88.4%, as the figure shows.

The increase from each extra evaluator shrinks, from 22.8 points for the second to 14.7 for the third and 9.6 for the fourth, which is why most teams use three to five evaluators and not twenty. The figures assume independence, and real evaluators overlap more than that, so they are best taken as optimistic.

lead.text: Not every problem deserves the same effort, so each is given a **severity rating**. Nielsen's scale runs from 0 to 4: 0 means the evaluator does not agree that it is a usability problem, 1 is cosmetic and to be fixed if time allows, 2 is minor, 3 is major and important to fix, and 4 is a usability catastrophe that must be fixed before release.

Three factors decide the rating. **Frequency** asks how many users meet the problem, **impact** asks how hard it is for them to overcome, and **persistence** asks whether they will be caught by it every time or learn to avoid it. A mislabelled button that every user meets on every visit and cannot avoid rates higher than a typo on a settings page that few see.

afterFigure.text: Ratings from a single evaluator are unreliable, so the group averages its members' ratings when it merges the lists, and the average is used to order the fixes.

lead.text: The **cognitive walkthrough**, described by Wharton, Rieman, Lewis and Polson in 1994, inspects an interface for how easily a new user can learn it. The evaluator takes a task, lists the actions that the interface requires, and at each action asks four questions. Will the user try to achieve the right effect? Will the user notice that the correct action is available? Will the user connect the correct action with the effect they want? If the action is taken, will the user see that progress is being made towards the goal?

A heuristic evaluation looks at a whole screen and asks which rules it breaks, whereas a walkthrough looks at one task path and asks where a first-time user would go wrong. The four questions correspond to the gulfs of the earlier lesson: the first three concern execution, and the fourth concerns evaluation.

reveal.text: Whether a new user would try for the right effect, notice the right action, connect it with that effect and see progress afterwards. The first three are about acting, and the last is about reading the result.

lead.text: A heuristic evaluation needs evaluators and an interface or a mock-up, and no users, so it fits a week with no participants. A cognitive walkthrough fits a design for first-time users, such as a sign-up flow. A usability test or a tree test needs participants and finds what real people do, which no inspection can promise.
Whatever the method, the output is a list of problems with severities, and the severities set the order of the work.

reveal.text: Weaker evaluators cost more people for the same coverage, which is a reason to use experienced evaluators and to supplement the review with a test.

blocks.text: In a heuristic evaluation, a few people who know the ten heuristics go through an interface screen by screen and note every place where it breaks one, without a single user taking part. Nielsen reports that one evaluator working alone typically finds around a third of the problems, but different evaluators find different problems, so the useful question is what a small group finds between them.
Inspection is the cheapest kind of usability evaluation, since it needs no participants and works on a mock-up, but it produces a long list of problems of very different weight.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to estimate what a group of evaluators finds, rate a problem on the 0 to 4 scale, and choose between a heuristic evaluation and a walkthrough.
intro.whyItMatters: Inspection is quick and cheap, and severity tells a team what to fix first.

recap.keyIdea: Evaluators inspect alone and merge their findings, a group of n finds 1 − (1 − L)^n of the problems, severity from 0 to 4 sets the order of repair, and a walkthrough asks four questions at each action of a task.

blocks.text: You worked out that two evaluators who each find 35% together find 57.8% and three find 72.5%, and that the gain from each addition shrinks. Severity combines frequency, impact and persistence into a rating from 0 to 4, and a cognitive walkthrough looks at one task path with four questions at each action. Inspection finds problems before a test, and does not replace one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson narrows to the places where most users meet trouble: forms, error messages and the feedback that follows an action.

lessons.title: Forms, errors and feedback

reveal.text: It makes the error impossible. The next screen sets out the ways of preventing errors.

lead.text: Psychologists distinguish two kinds of error, and both occur in forms. In a **slip** the user has the right goal and performs the wrong action, as when a finger hits the wrong key, and in a **mistake** the goal or the plan is wrong, as when the user has misunderstood what a field asks for.

Prevention comes first, because it removes the error and does not have to describe it. A **constraint** limits the options to valid ones, as a calendar picker does for dates and a numeric keypad does for a phone number. A **default** supplies a sensible value so that most users do not have to type or choose anything, and **formatting help**, such as an example beside a field or automatic spacing in a card number, lets the user see the expected shape before making an error.

reveal.text: The general name is a constraint. It is the strongest form of prevention, because the wrong action is simply not available.

lead.text: Some errors cannot be prevented, and then the message has to carry the whole repair. A good message has three parts: it says **what happened**, it says **why**, and it says **what to do next**, in the user's words and not the system's, so "The email address is missing an @. Enter it like name@example.com." in place of "Invalid input." It sits next to the field it concerns, and the field is also marked in a way that does not rely on colour alone.

With no message, the user has to find the problem unaided, and with a general message at the top of the page they must read it, then look for the field, and then work out what is wrong. With a message beside the field, the three parts are in the place where the user is already looking.

afterFigure.text: The message is also where accessibility begins: success criterion 3.3.1, Error Identification, in WCAG 2.2, requires that an error in an input be identified and described to the user in text.

steps.headline: Rewrite the message 'Invalid input.' for an email field, one part at a time.

workedSteps.text: "Invalid input." can be checked against the three parts of a good message: what happened, why, and what to do next.
The repair adds what happened and why, in the user's words: "The email address is missing an @."
It then adds what to do next, with an example of a valid value: "Enter it like name@example.com."
The message goes directly under the Email field, and the field itself is marked as well as the text.

reveal.text: The good message names the field, gives the rule and the user's count, and so lets the user act without guessing.

lead.text: A confirmation dialog, "Are you sure?", looks like protection, and it works poorly for actions that are meant. Users who see the dialog on every deletion answer it by habit, and the one time it matters they click through it. A reversible action with an **undo**, as Gmail offers for a few seconds after sending a message, costs nothing when the action was intended and rescues the user when it was not.

Confirmation still has a place for actions that cannot be reversed, such as permanently deleting an account, and then the dialog should say exactly what will be lost, with a button named for the action and not "OK". Elsewhere, undo is the better design.

reveal.text: Reversal after the action, and no dialog before it, is the pattern that works for reversible actions.

lead.text: A form's behaviour rests on its markup. A visible **label** element, tied to its field by the for and id attributes, gives the field a name that stays on screen and is announced by a screen reader, and clicking it moves focus to the field. An **in-field hint** is text inside the field that disappears when typing begins, so it is not a replacement for a label.

The **type** attribute lets the browser check the shape of a value, so `type="email"` asks for something that looks like an address, and **required** makes the browser reject an empty field. **autocomplete** says what the field is for, so that the browser can fill it in, and WCAG 2.2 also asks, in criterion 3.3.7, that a form not make users enter the same information twice in one process.

afterFigure.text: Validation can run when the user leaves a field, which is inline validation and avoids a wall of errors at the end, but it should not fire while the user is still typing an address that is not yet complete.

reveal.text: Limits can be permanent, temporary or situational, and each group is larger than people expect. The next screen starts with how WCAG organises its requirements.

lead.text: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are published by the World Wide Web Consortium. Every requirement is a **success criterion** with a number, and the criteria sit under four principles, which spell **POUR**: content must be **Perceivable**, so that users can sense it, **Operable**, so that they can work it, **Understandable**, so that they can follow it, and **Robust**, so that different browsers and assistive technologies can interpret it.

Each criterion also has a level. **Level A** is the basic requirement, **AA** adds the requirements that most laws and policies call for, and **AAA** is the strictest, and rarely required in full for a whole site. When a policy says that a site must conform to WCAG 2.2, it usually means all the A and AA criteria.

reveal.text: That concerns the controls, and the principle that covers whether controls can be worked is Operable.

lead.text: Every colour has a **relative luminance** L, a number from 0 for black to 1 for white that estimates how much light it gives out as the eye perceives it. The **contrast ratio** of two colours is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the lighter colour's luminance and L2 the darker's. The 0.05 stands for the light that always reaches the eye from the surroundings. Black on white gives (1 + 0.05) / (0 + 0.05) = 21, the largest value possible, and two identical colours give 1.

To find L for a colour from its red, green and blue values, each channel is divided by 255 and then linearised, and the results are combined as L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B. For #767676 each channel is 118 out of 255, which linearises to about 0.181, so L is 0.181 and the ratio against white is 1.05 / 0.231, about 4.54. The figure places four pairs on the scale.

afterFigure.text: The weights differ because the eye is most sensitive to green and least to blue, so a pure blue on white gives a ratio of about 8.6 while a pure green is lighter and gives much less.

steps.headline: Compute the contrast ratio for L1 = 0.5 and L2 = 0.05, then for L1 = 0.8 and L2 = 0.2.

workedSteps.text: Add 0.05 to each luminance, so that the numerator is 0.55 and the denominator is 0.10.
Divide the numerator by the denominator.
The ratio of 5.5 is above 4.5, so the pair passes AA for normal text.
Now take L1 = 0.8 and L2 = 0.2.

reveal.text: The result is 16, below the 21 that black on white gives, which is the top of the scale. Any real pair of colours falls between 1 and 21.

lead.text: Under criterion 1.4.3, Contrast (Minimum), text must have a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1, except that **large text**, which is 18 point or larger, or 14 point bold or larger, needs only 3 to 1, because bigger letters are easier to read. Under criterion 1.4.11, Non-text Contrast, the parts of controls that a user needs to see, such as the border of a text field, and the key parts of graphics need at least 3 to 1 against their surroundings. Level AAA asks for 7 to 1 for normal text.
The tests are exact. WCAG says that the computed values should not be rounded, so a ratio of 4.499 fails and the pair #777777 on white, at 4.48, fails by a hair.

reveal.text: The lower figure is the same one that applies to the parts of controls under 1.4.11.

lead.text: Criterion 1.4.1, Use of Color, says that colour must not be the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action or distinguishing an element. A link that differs from the text around it only by hue is invisible to a reader who cannot tell the two hues apart, and an error shown only as red text cannot be seen by them either.

The repair is to add a second cue that does not depend on colour, such as an underline for links and a mark or a word for errors. Contrast and colour use are both about whether people can perceive what is on the screen, and both fall under Perceivable.

blocks.text: The text colour #767676 on a white background gives a contrast ratio of 4.54 to 1, and the colour #777777, one step lighter in each channel, gives 4.48 to 1. The two greys look the same to almost everyone, and yet the first meets the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines at level AA for normal text and the second does not, because the line is drawn at 4.5 and WCAG says that computed values must not be rounded.
That precision is possible because the guidelines turn a vague wish, text that can be read, into numbers that can be checked.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the four WCAG principles, compute a contrast ratio from two luminance values, and judge whether a colour pair meets AA.
intro.whyItMatters: Contrast turns readable into a number a designer can check in seconds.

recap.keyIdea: WCAG 2.2 groups its criteria under Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust, at levels A, AA and AAA, and AA needs a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text and key interface parts.

blocks.text: You computed contrast ratios from two relative luminances, found that black on white gives 21 and that 4.48 fails where 4.54 passes, and saw that the ratio is never rounded. A meaning carried by colour alone fails readers who cannot see the difference, so a second cue is added.

lead.text: WCAG success criterion 2.1.1 requires that all functionality be operable through a keyboard interface, and that is level A. The Tab key moves **focus** from one interactive element to the next, and Enter or Space activates it. Native links, buttons and form fields are in the Tab order by default. A div or a span with an onclick handler is not, and ignores Enter and Space as well, so it works for a mouse user and for no one else.

Two further criteria concern focus itself. Criterion 2.4.7, Focus Visible, requires a visible indicator of where focus is, which is why removing the outline with CSS and supplying nothing in its place is a failure. Criterion 2.4.11, Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), which is new in WCAG 2.2, requires that the focused element is not entirely hidden behind other content such as a sticky header or a cookie banner.

lead.text: A screen reader does not see the page as the eye does. It reads the markup, and for each control it announces a name, a role and a state, such as "Save, button" or "Email, edit text, required". Criterion 4.1.2, Name, Role, Value, requires these to be available to assistive technology. A native **button** supplies them automatically, and a div supplies none unless a role, a name, key handling and focus are all added by hand, which is more work and easier to get wrong.

A **label** tied to its field gives the field its name. **Headings** from h1 down form an outline that screen reader users move through, so they should follow the structure of the content and not the size the designer wants. Links, which go to another page, use the a element with an href, and buttons, which do something on this page, use button.

steps.headline: Choose the element for each control on a product page.

workedSteps.text: The Add to basket control changes the basket and stays on the page, so it performs an action. The element is a button.
The Delivery information control opens a different page.
The field for a postcode needs a name that a screen reader can announce, which a label tied to the field provides.

lead.text: Criterion 1.1.1, Non-text Content, asks for a text alternative for non-text content, and the right text depends on what the image is for. An **informative** image carries a message, so its alt text states that message, as for a chart that shows sales rising. A **functional** image is used as a control, as with a magnifier icon in a search button, and its alt text names what the control does, here Search, and not what it looks like. A **decorative** image carries nothing, and it takes an empty alt attribute, `alt=""`, so that a screen reader skips it.

Adding descriptive text to every image is a mistake, because a decorative flourish read aloud as "wavy line" slows the user and says nothing. An image with no alt attribute at all is worse, since some screen readers then read the file name.

lead.text: Small targets are hard to hit for anyone with a tremor, a large thumb or a moving bus, and Fitts's law says why: a small W makes the index of difficulty larger. Criterion 2.5.8, Target Size (Minimum), new in WCAG 2.2 at level AA, requires that pointer targets be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. A smaller target passes if a 24 pixel circle centred on it does not meet another target, which is the **spacing exception**.

The enhanced criterion 2.5.5, at level AAA, asks for 44 by 44 CSS pixels, and it is a sound aim for important controls. Links inside a sentence are exempt from both, since their height follows the text around them.

lead.text: Criterion 1.4.4, Resize Text, requires that text can be resized to 200% without losing content or function, and 1.4.10, Reflow, requires that a page can be viewed at a width of 320 CSS pixels without scrolling in two directions. A layout of fixed-width columns fails the second, while one that stacks at narrow widths passes it, which is also what a phone needs.

A short audit therefore runs in a fixed order. Unplug the mouse and Tab through the page, then check that each control is a native element with a name, that images have the right alt, that fields have labels, that targets are at least 24 pixels, and that the page reflows at 320 pixels.

reveal.text: Four: the image has no alt, the field has no label, and the div and the span cannot be reached from a keyboard. The button and the link are already correct.

lessons.orientation: Checking keyboard operation, semantic elements, alt text and target size.
lessons.nextAction: You can now check a colour pair, a touch target and a form against the main WCAG 2.2 criteria.

blocks.text: Unplug the mouse and press Tab repeatedly on a page. Focus moves from one control to the next, and every control that focus reaches can be used with Enter or Space. A control that focus skips cannot be used at all, and the page may look perfect while a quarter of its buttons are out of reach. For a person who cannot use a mouse, or who uses a screen reader, that is the whole of the interface.

The cause is nearly always in the markup. A button built from a div with a click handler looks the same as a real button and behaves differently, and the difference stays hidden until someone tries to reach it from the keyboard or hears it read by a screen reader.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to check markup for keyboard operation, choose the right native element, write the right alt text, and test a target against the 24 px minimum.
intro.whyItMatters: A page that looks perfect can still be unusable without a mouse.

recap.keyIdea: A page is accessible to a keyboard when its controls are native elements in the Tab order with visible focus, its images have the alt text their job needs, and its pointer targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels.

blocks.text: You saw that a div with a click handler is not focusable and has no role, whereas a button supplies focus, a role and key handling, and that alt text depends on whether an image informs, functions or only decorates. Criterion 2.5.8 sets the AA target at 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with a spacing exception, and a short audit combines these checks with contrast and form labels.

questions.prompt: Six identical dots stand in a row. The gaps between neighbouring dots, from left to right, are 8 px, 40 px, 8 px, 40 px and 8 px. How will a viewer see them?
hints: Each gap is either small, which joins neighbours, or large, which separates them.
Every 40 px gap marks a boundary between groups, and there are two of them.
questions.onCorrect: The 8 px gaps join neighbours and the two 40 px gaps separate the pairs, so the row is read as three groups of two.

misconceptions.feedback: One unbroken row would need gaps that are roughly equal. Here two of the gaps are five times the others, and each of them breaks the row.
Six separate dots would need every gap to be large. The 8 px gaps are small beside the 40 px gaps, so they join their neighbours.
Two groups of three would need one wide gap in the middle. There are two wide gaps here, after the second dot and after the fourth.

choices.label: As one row of six dots

questions.prompt: On a settings page every control is 24 px from its neighbours, and a pale panel sits behind just three of them: font size, line spacing and theme. Which cue makes those three read as a group?
hints: The gaps are all equal, so look for what the three controls share that the others do not.
The panel is a boundary around the three controls.
questions.onCorrect: A shared panel or outline makes elements read as one unit, and it can outweigh a gap between them.

misconceptions.feedback: Proximity compares gaps, and here every control is the same 24 px from its neighbours, so distance cannot single out the three.
Similarity needs the elements to look alike, and nothing about the three controls is said to differ from the rest. What sets them apart is the panel behind them.

questions.prompt: By how many px is the label nearer to the wrong field than to its own?
hints: The label is 8 px from the field above and 24 px from its own field.
Subtract the smaller gap from the larger.
24 minus 8.
questions.onCorrect: The label is 24 px from its own field and 8 px from the wrong one, a difference of 16 px.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 px is the gap to the wrong field. The question asks how much nearer that is than the gap to its own field.
24 px is the gap to its own field. Subtract the gap to the wrong field from it.
Adding the gaps gives 32 px. The question asks for the difference.

questions.prompt: On a news page the photo is the largest and darkest element, so readers look at it before the headline. The ranking that puts the photo first is the page's visual ____.
hints: The word names a ranking from most to least prominent.
It is the same word used for an organisation chart.
questions.onCorrect: Visual hierarchy ranks elements by how strongly they draw the eye, and a squint shows that ranking.

misconceptions.feedback: Proximity and grouping decide what belongs together. The question asks about the order of attention.
