questions.prompt: Four buttons stand in a row with equal gaps of 8 px between neighbours. A panel is then drawn around the first two buttons and another around the last two. How does a viewer now read the row?
hints: Distance says nothing here, because all the gaps are equal.
An outline drawn around elements is the strongest of the grouping cues.

acceptedIdeas: As two pairs, one in each panel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As two pairs, one in each panel

questions.onCorrect: Each panel is a common region, which joins the two buttons inside it even though every gap is the same.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal gaps would make one row if nothing else were present, but the panels are an outline, and common region outweighs proximity.
The gaps are only 8 px, so nothing pushes the buttons apart, and each panel joins the two inside it.

choices.label: As two pairs, one in each panel
As one row of four, since the gaps are still equal

questions.prompt: Two buttons sit 8 px apart, and a third sits 40 px from them. With no other cues, which reading is most likely?
hints: Compare the 8 px gap with the 40 px gap.
The smaller gap joins elements and the larger gap separates them.

acceptedIdeas: The first two form a group and the third stands apart
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first two form a group and the third stands apart

choices.label: All three form one group, since they stand in a row
The first two form a group and the third stands apart
Three separate buttons, with no grouping at all
The last two form a group, with the first set apart

questions.onCorrect: The 8 px gap is much smaller than the 40 px gap, so proximity joins the first two and sets the third apart.

misconceptions.feedback: Three separate buttons would need equal, large gaps. Here two of them are only 8 px apart.
The last two are the pair that sits farthest apart, 40 px, so they are not joined.
All three would need roughly equal gaps. The 40 px gap is five times the 8 px gap.

questions.prompt: Two buttons are given the same green fill, and the reader takes them to belong together whatever the distance between them. This cue is called ____.
hints: Elements that look alike are read as members of one set.
The word starts with the same letters as "similar".
questions.onCorrect: Similarity groups by shared colour, shape or size, and it also tells the viewer that the elements are alike in meaning.

misconceptions.feedback: Proximity concerns the gaps. This cue works at any distance because the buttons look alike.

questions.prompt: A page uses red for error text and also for a decorative heading. What does the repeated colour tell the viewer?
hints: Similarity asserts that things which look alike are alike.
Red has already been used for one purpose on this page.

choices.label: Nothing, because colour carries no meaning
The heading is more important than the error

questions.onCorrect: Once red has marked errors, the viewer reads any red text as belonging to that set, so the heading looks like an error.

misconceptions.feedback: Colour carries meaning once it has been used consistently. A viewer who has seen red errors will read red as an error.
Red text on this page has been used for errors, so the viewer reads it as one, not as a sign of rank.
Nothing on the page has linked red to links or buttons. The only meaning red has acquired is error.

questions.prompt: A 16-digit card number is shown as four groups of four digits, and each group is learned as one unit. How many units must a person hold?
hints: Count the groups, not the digits.
Four groups of four digits make sixteen digits.
Each group counts once.
questions.onCorrect: Each group of four is held as one unit, so a sixteen-digit number costs four units, which is about the span working memory handles.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every digit. Grouping lets each group of four stand as one unit.
Two digits per unit would give eight, but the groups here hold four digits each.

questions.prompt: A person reads a list of unrelated items once and then has to repeat them straight away. Roughly how many separate items can most people hold in mind like this?
hints: Think of how many digits of a new phone number you can keep while you dial.
The eleven digits in the opening example were too many for most people.

acceptedIdeas: A handful, somewhere between about four and seven
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A handful, somewhere between about four and seven

questions.onCorrect: Estimates run from about seven, in George Miller's paper of 1956, down to about four in later work, and either way the store is small.

misconceptions.feedback: Most people hold more than three. Studies place the limit at a handful of items, and grouping lets each item carry more.
Careful reading does not stretch the store. Twenty unrelated items is far beyond what people can repeat after one reading.
Reading time helps a little, but the store that holds items for immediate use is small however long the reading took.

choices.label: As many as the person had time to read
Only two or three, however simple the items
A handful, somewhere between about four and seven
Around twenty, if the person reads carefully

questions.prompt: Most readers hold the year 1989 in mind as a single unit, although it has four digits. That unit is called a ____.
hints: The word names a piece cut from a larger whole.
The lesson's title for the process of making these units begins with the same word.
questions.onCorrect: A chunk can be a single digit or a whole familiar phrase, so the same capacity holds more when items are grouped meaningfully.

misconceptions.feedback: An item is a single piece. The question asks for the unit made by grouping items.

questions.prompt: A settings page has a menu of forty options, and users complain that finding one is hard. What kind of problem is this most likely to be?
hints: Ask whether the user has to produce anything from memory.
Every option is visible on screen.

acceptedIdeas: A search problem, since every option is visible and the user must scan
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A search problem, since every option is visible and the user must scan

choices.label: A recall problem, since users must remember the order of the menu
A search problem, since every option is visible and the user must scan
No problem, since menus use recognition
A recall problem, since forty is far beyond working memory

questions.onCorrect: A long menu keeps recognition, because every option is on screen, but it costs scanning time, so the fix is grouping and ordering and not memory aids.

misconceptions.feedback: Working memory limits how many items a person holds at once, and a visible menu does not have to be held in mind.
Users do not need the order in memory, since the options stay on screen.
The menu does use recognition, but forty options still take time to scan, so a problem remains.

questions.prompt: How many fewer things does the person hold when the eleven digits are grouped?
hints: Ungrouped, each digit is a separate item.
Grouped as 077 009 001 23 there are four chunks.
11 minus 4.
questions.onCorrect: Eleven separate digits become four chunks, a saving of 7.

misconceptions.feedback: Four is the number of chunks. The question asks for the saving.
Eleven is the number of digits before grouping.

questions.prompt: A checkout asks the user to type a six-digit code that was shown on the previous page as 482 915. How many chunks must the user keep in mind while changing pages?
hints: Each group of three counts as one chunk.
Six digits in two groups.
Count the groups.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two groups of three, so 2 chunks.

questions.onCorrect: Two chunks have to be carried across the page change, and showing the code on the same page would reduce that to none.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts each digit. The groups of three are held as one chunk each.
Three is the group size. Count the groups.

questions.prompt: A 20-character licence key is displayed as 4F7K-29QM-X4PL-82DR-ZT6B. How many chunks must a user hold to type it from memory?
hints: Each group of four counts as one chunk.
Five groups of four make twenty characters.
Count the groups, not the characters.
questions.onCorrect: Five chunks is more than the roughly four that working memory holds, so the key should stay visible, with a copy button, instead of being memorised.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every character. The groups of four are held as one chunk each.
Four is the size of each group. The number of groups is five.

questions.prompt: A phone number is displayed as 020 7946 0958. How many chunks does it have?
hints: Look at where the spaces are.
Each space-separated group is one chunk.
Count the groups.
questions.onCorrect: The display splits the ten digits into three groups, so a reader holds three chunks and not ten digits.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the digits. The spaces mark three groups, each held as one chunk.
Four is the size of the middle group. The count of groups is three.

questions.prompt: Producing an answer with no cue on screen at all is called ____.
hints: The other half of the pair is recognition.
It needs the most from memory.
questions.onCorrect: Recall must produce the item from memory alone, which is why a blank command prompt is harder to use than a menu.

misconceptions.feedback: Recognition picks from options that are shown. The question describes having no cue.

questions.prompt: Which design relies on recognition rather than recall?
hints: Which option puts the answer choices on screen?

acceptedIdeas: Choosing a country from a dropdown list
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Choosing a country from a dropdown list

choices.label: Typing a country code from memory
Choosing a country from a dropdown list

questions.onCorrect: A dropdown shows the options, so the user only has to recognise the right one.

misconceptions.feedback: A typed code has to be produced from memory, so it is recall.
A PIN is held in memory and typed with no cue, so it is recall.
A username is produced from memory, so it is recall.

questions.prompt: A target is 1 cm wide and 7 cm away. Which change makes it easier to hit: halving the distance to 3.5 cm, or doubling the width to 2 cm?
hints: Difficulty depends on the ratio of distance to width.
Work out D divided by W in each case.

acceptedIdeas: They help by exactly the same amount
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They help by exactly the same amount

choices.label: They help by exactly the same amount
Neither changes how hard it is

questions.onCorrect: Both changes make D/W equal to 3.5, so they give the same index of difficulty. Distance and width matter only through their ratio.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving D gives D/W = 3.5. Doubling W also gives 3.5, so neither helps more.
Doubling W gives D/W = 3.5, and halving D gives the same 3.5, so neither wins.
Both changes reduce D/W from 7 to 3.5, so both make the target easier.

questions.prompt: What is ID now, in bits, to two decimal places?
hints: Compute D/W first: 14 divided by 7.
Add 1 to the ratio before taking the logarithm.
ID = log2(3).
questions.onCorrect: Widening from 2 cm to 7 cm cuts the index of difficulty from 3 bits to about 1.58 bits.

misconceptions.feedback: That is D/W. The index of difficulty is the base-2 logarithm of D/W + 1.
That is log2(2). The formula adds 1 to the ratio before taking the logarithm, so the argument is 3.

questions.prompt: A target is 2 cm wide and 6 cm away. What is ID = log2(D/W + 1), in bits?
hints: Compute D/W: 6 divided by 2.
Add 1 to that ratio.
The logarithm is base 2, and 2 raised to what power gives 4?
questions.onCorrect: D/W is 3, and log2(3 + 1) = log2(4) = 2 bits.

misconceptions.feedback: That is D/W. Add 1 and then take the base-2 logarithm.
That is log2(3). The formula uses D/W + 1, which is 4.
That is D/W + 1. The index of difficulty takes the base-2 logarithm of it.

questions.prompt: A button at the very top edge of the screen is easy to hit because the pointer stops there, which makes the target act as if it were unlimited in ____ (one word, along the direction of travel).
hints: The pointer moving upward cannot go beyond the edge.
Width in Fitts's law means size along the line of motion.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Height: the target is effectively infinitely tall.

questions.onCorrect: The edge stops the pointer, so overshooting costs nothing and the target's size along the movement counts as unlimited.

questions.prompt: A menu has 7 equally likely items. What is log2(n + 1)?
hints: Add 1 to n first.
log2(8) asks what power of 2 gives 8.
questions.onCorrect: log2(7 + 1) = log2(8) = 3, so seven equally likely items give 3 units of the decision term.

misconceptions.feedback: That is log2(7). Hick's law uses n + 1, which is 8.
Seven is n. The question asks for the logarithm of n + 1.
That is n + 1. Take the base-2 logarithm of it.

questions.prompt: A list of 15 equally likely items grows to 31. By how much does log2(n + 1) increase?
hints: Work out log2(16) and log2(32).
Subtract.
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the list from 15 to 31 items adds one unit, from 4 to 5, so the decision term grows by a constant step for each doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That would double the term. Each doubling of the list adds one unit.
That is the increase in the number of items. The question asks about the logarithm.

questions.prompt: A target is 1 cm wide and 15 cm away. What is ID = log2(D/W + 1), in bits?
hints: Compute D/W first.
Add 1, then take the base-2 logarithm.
questions.onCorrect: D/W is 15, and log2(15 + 1) = log2(16) = 4 bits.

misconceptions.feedback: That is log2(15). The formula adds 1 first, which makes 16.
That is D/W. Add 1 and take the base-2 logarithm.
That is D/W + 1. The index of difficulty is its base-2 logarithm.

questions.prompt: A menu has 15 equally likely items. What is log2(n + 1)?
hints: Add 1 to n.
What power of 2 gives 16?
questions.onCorrect: log2(15 + 1) = log2(16) = 4, one more than for 7 items, because the list has doubled.

misconceptions.feedback: That is log2(15). Hick's law uses n + 1, which is 16.
Fifteen is n. Take the logarithm of n + 1.
That is n + 1. Take its base-2 logarithm.

questions.prompt: Why is a button at the screen's top edge easy to hit with a mouse?
hints: Think about what happens to a pointer that moves past the target.
Fitts's law uses the target's size along the direction of motion.

acceptedIdeas: The pointer stops at the edge, so the target is effectively very tall
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pointer stops at the edge, so the target is effectively very tall

choices.label: An edge is nearer to where the pointer starts, so the distance D is smaller
An edge button has fewer neighbours, so Hick's law makes the choice quicker
The pointer stops at the edge, so the target is effectively very tall
Users look at the edges of a screen first, so they notice the button sooner

questions.onCorrect: The pointer cannot overshoot the edge, so the target's size along the line of motion is effectively unlimited.

misconceptions.feedback: Where people look affects how fast they find a button, which is not what Fitts's law measures. The law is about the movement of the pointer.
Hick's law is about choosing among options. Pointing difficulty is Fitts's law.
An edge is not generally nearer than other places, so distance does not explain the advantage.

questions.prompt: Two doors both open by being pushed. One has a flat metal plate at hand height and the other has a vertical handle. Which door is more likely to need a sign saying PUSH?
hints: Imagine reaching for each door without reading anything.
Ask what a hand naturally does with a handle.
questions.onCorrect: A handle invites a grip and a pull, so on a door that must be pushed it tells people the wrong thing, and the sign is there to correct it.

misconceptions.feedback: A flat plate offers nothing to grip, so the only thing a hand can do with it is push, which is what the door needs.
The doors behave alike, but they do not look alike, and people act on what the door shows them.

choices.label: The door with the flat plate
Both equally, since both open the same way

questions.prompt: On a touch screen, a row of three short lines at the edge of a card shows that the card can be dragged. A cue of this kind is called a ____.
hints: The word is built from the verb to signify.
It is the visible cue, and not the thing the object allows.
questions.onCorrect: Norman introduced signifier in the 2013 edition of The Design of Everyday Things for the perceivable cue, apart from what the object permits.

misconceptions.feedback: An affordance is what the object allows. The question asks for the perceivable cue that shows where to act.

questions.prompt: A user wants to crop a photo, and the crop command is kept inside a menu called Transform that they never think to open. Which gulf is this?
hints: Ask whether the trouble comes before the user acts or after.
The user cannot work out which action to take.
questions.onCorrect: The gap lies between the user's goal and the actions the screen makes visible, which is the gulf of execution, and a visible Crop command would narrow it.

misconceptions.feedback: The gulf of evaluation lies after an action, in reading what the system did. This user has not yet been able to act.
The command may work, but the user cannot see which action matches the goal, and that gap is part of the design.

choices.label: Neither, since the command works once the user finds it

questions.prompt: A washing machine's display shows only the programme the user chose. The user presses Start and the machine begins to wash, but the display does not change. Which gulf does the display leave open?
hints: Ask whether the user's trouble comes before they act or after.
Think about what the display tells the user once the machine is running.
questions.onCorrect: The display shows the programme and not the state of the machine, so the user cannot tell what it is doing, which is the gulf of evaluation.

misconceptions.feedback: The user found Start and pressed it, so the action was available and visible. The gap lies in reading what the machine is doing afterwards.
The user did act correctly, but a display that never shows what the machine is doing still leaves them unable to tell whether it is working, and that gap belongs to the design.

choices.label: Neither, since the user pressed the right button

questions.prompt: A door can be pushed, and that is what it permits regardless of what it looks like. The thing a door permits is called its ____.
hints: James Gibson coined the word in 1979.
It is what the object allows, as distinct from the cue that shows it.
questions.onCorrect: An affordance is a relation between an object and a person, so a door affords pushing whether or not anything on it says so.

misconceptions.feedback: The signifier is the visible cue. The question asks for what the door permits.

questions.prompt: A user cannot find the Export command and says, "I am just not good with computers." According to the two gulfs, where does the gap that stopped them lie?
hints: A gulf is a gap that a designer can narrow.
Think about who controls the system image.

acceptedIdeas: In the design, which did not make the command visible where the user looks
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the design, which did not make the command visible where the user looks

questions.onCorrect: Both gulfs depend on what the system shows and offers, so a user who falls into one has met a design problem that others will meet as well.

misconceptions.feedback: Users differ in experience, but a gulf is a gap in what the screen shows and offers, and that is something the designer controls.
Exporting is an ordinary task, and what stopped this user was finding the command. What a screen makes visible is something the designer can change.

choices.label: In the design, which did not make the command visible where the user looks
In the user, who has not yet learned how programs are organised
In the task, since exporting is too advanced for a beginner

questions.prompt: A user taps 'Save', and nothing on screen changes. Which gulf is this?
hints: The user acted. What is missing?
Evaluation concerns perceiving and interpreting the system's state.
questions.onCorrect: The action may have worked, but nothing shows it, so the user cannot judge the result, which is the gulf of evaluation.

misconceptions.feedback: The Save button was found and pressed, so the action was available. The gap comes after the action.
A gap exists: the user cannot tell whether the save happened.
Only one stage fails here. The user found the action but cannot read its result.

questions.prompt: A cue that shows where an action can be taken, such as a button's raised edge, is called a ____.
hints: It is the visible part, as opposed to what is permitted.
questions.onCorrect: A signifier is perceivable, and designers add or remove it, whereas the affordance is what the object allows.

misconceptions.feedback: An affordance is what the object allows. The question asks for the visible cue.

questions.prompt: A user cannot find which menu holds 'Export'. Which gulf is this?
hints: The user knows the goal and cannot find the action.
Execution is about acting.
questions.onCorrect: The goal is clear and the way to act on it is hidden, which is the gulf of execution.

misconceptions.feedback: The user has not acted yet, so there is no result to evaluate.
There is a gap between the goal and the available action, so it is not neither.
Only the stage before acting fails, since nothing has happened yet to evaluate.

questions.prompt: A team wants to know whether people can find things with its new search. Which question is more likely to give an honest answer?
hints: Look for the question that assumes an answer.
One question asks about something the person has done.

acceptedIdeas: How did you find the last thing you looked for?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How did you find the last thing you looked for?

choices.label: How did you find the last thing you looked for?
Neither, since interviews cannot ask about search
How much do you like the new search?

questions.onCorrect: Asking about a particular past event gets behaviour, while asking how much they like something assumes they do and invites politeness.

misconceptions.feedback: The wording assumes the person likes the feature, and it pushes towards a high rating whatever happened.
The wordings differ in what they assume, and one invites a polite answer.
Interviews are well suited to questions about specific past experiences.

questions.prompt: A team asks fifty users which new features they would like, and builds the three that were requested most often. How well are those answers likely to predict which features people then use?
hints: Think about how often a plan you described matched what you later did.
The question asks people to predict, not to report.

acceptedIdeas: Only loosely, since people predict their own behaviour poorly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only loosely, since people predict their own behaviour poorly

questions.onCorrect: What people say they would do often differs from what they then do, so a question about a past event is a firmer guide than a request for wishes.

misconceptions.feedback: People know what annoys them, but asked to design a feature they guess, and what they say they would use often differs from what they later do.
The answers are not random, since they reflect real wishes and real frustrations. They are weak evidence of future behaviour, which is a different thing.

choices.label: Very well, since people know best what they will want to use
Not at all, since users answer these questions at random
Only loosely, since people predict their own behaviour poorly

questions.prompt: A question whose wording suggests the answer wanted, such as "Don't you agree the new menu is easier?", is called a ____ question.
hints: The question leads the respondent towards an answer.
questions.onCorrect: A leading question builds the wanted answer into the wording, which turns the reply into agreement and not evidence.

questions.prompt: A survey asks employees whether they exercise regularly, and the answers are more flattering than the building's gym records suggest. Which source of bias best explains the gap?
hints: Ask whether the error would shrink with more respondents.
Exercise is a habit people like to be seen to have.
questions.onCorrect: People tend to report a worthy habit more often than they practise it, which is social desirability bias, and a larger sample would not remove it.

misconceptions.feedback: Self-selection concerns who chooses to answer. Here the problem is in what people say about themselves, since regular exercise is a habit people like to claim.
The question as described does not suggest an answer. The push towards a flattering reply comes from the respondents.
Chance error moves answers both ways and averages out. These answers lean consistently in the flattering direction.

questions.prompt: What is the margin of error for n = 2,500, in percentage points to one decimal place?
hints: The standard deviation part is sqrt(0.25 / 2500).
Multiply 1.96 by 0.01 and convert to percentage points.
questions.onCorrect: Four times the sample halves the margin, from 3.9 points to 2.0 points.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the margin for n = 625. With four times as many responses the square root halves it.
That is the proportion. The question asks for percentage points, so multiply by 100.
That is the square root as a percentage. The margin multiplies it by 1.96.

questions.prompt: A survey of n = 100 finds that p = 0.2 prefer a feature. What is the 95% margin of error in percentage points, to one decimal place?
hints: Divide 0.16 by 100, then take the square root.
questions.onCorrect: A proportion further from 0.5 has a smaller margin, 7.8 points here against 9.8 at p = 0.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the margin for p = 0.5. Here p(1 − p) = 0.16, not 0.25.
That is the proportion. The question asks for percentage points.

questions.prompt: A survey of n = 250 has a margin of 6.2 points, and the team wants to halve it. How many respondents are needed?
hints: The margin depends on the square root of n.
To halve a square root, multiply n by a factor whose square root is 2.
Four times the sample.
questions.onCorrect: Halving the margin takes four times the sample, which is why precision gets expensive quickly.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the sample only cuts the margin by about 29 percent, since the margin depends on the square root of n.
Eight times the sample would cut the margin to about a third.

questions.prompt: A survey of n = 900 gives p = 0.5. What is the 95% margin of error in percentage points, to one decimal place?
hints: That is about 0.01667.
questions.onCorrect: With n = 900 the standard error is 1.67 points and the margin 3.3 points.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the margin for n = 400. This sample is larger.
That is the margin for n = 100.

questions.prompt: Which question is not leading?
hints: Look for the wording that assumes no answer.
Three of the questions suggest what the asker hopes to hear.

acceptedIdeas: How would you describe finding a setting last week?
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How would you describe finding a setting last week?

choices.label: How would you describe finding a setting last week?
Don't you agree that the new menu is much easier to use?
How much did you love the redesigned settings page?
Isn't the old settings layout confusing to everyone?

questions.onCorrect: It asks about a specific past event and does not suggest how it went.

misconceptions.feedback: "Don't you agree" invites agreement.
The question asserts that the old layout is confusing.
The question presumes that the person loved the redesign.

questions.prompt: A bigger sample shrinks the margin of error but cannot fix a sample whose members chose themselves. The error that does not shrink with n is called ____.
hints: The margin of error describes chance variation.
The other kind of error is systematic.
questions.onCorrect: Bias pushes every response the same way, so more responses only make the wrong answer more precise.

misconceptions.feedback: Chance variation is what the margin of error measures, and it does shrink with n. The question asks about the error that does not.

questions.prompt: A menu offers 12 choices at the first level. Each of them opens another 12 choices, and each of those opens a final set of 12 items. Roughly how many items can this menu reach?
hints: Every one of the first 12 choices opens its own set of 12.
Two levels already reach 12 × 12 items.
questions.onCorrect: Each level multiplies the count by 12, so three levels reach 12 × 12 × 12 = 1,728 items.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding the levels, 12 + 12 + 12, gives 36, but each choice opens a whole new set of 12, so the counts multiply.
About 150 is what two levels reach, 12 × 12 = 144. The third level multiplies that by 12 again.
Each level multiplies the count by 12, and three such steps take it well past a few hundred.

questions.prompt: A team has no structure yet for a new help centre and wants to hear what categories people would invent for its 40 help articles. Which method fits?
hints: The team wants the participants to make up the categories.
One kind of card sort supplies the categories and the other does not.
questions.onCorrect: In an open card sort participants make the piles and name them, which gives the team both a grouping and the users' own words for it.

misconceptions.feedback: A tree test checks a structure that already exists, and this team has none yet.
A closed card sort gives participants the categories, so it cannot show which ones they would invent.

questions.prompt: What is this task's success rate, as a percentage?
hints: Success rate is the share of participants who reach the correct leaf.
Divide 18 by 24.
Write the proportion as a percentage by multiplying by 100.
questions.onCorrect: A success rate is the number who succeeded divided by the number who tried, so 18 of 24 is 75%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the proportion. The question asks for a percentage.
Six is the number who failed. Divide the successes by the total.

questions.prompt: Of 25 participants in a tree test, 20 reach the right leaf and 15 of the 25 go straight to it without backing up. What is directness, as a percentage of all participants?
hints: Directness counts the participants who went straight to the answer.
Divide 15 by 25.
questions.onCorrect: Directness is 15 of 25, which is 60%, lower than the 80% success rate, so some participants found the answer after wandering.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the success rate, 20 of 25. Directness counts only those who did not back up.
That divides 15 by 20. Directness is taken over all participants.

questions.prompt: A menu has 5 choices per level over 4 levels. How many items can it reach?
hints: Multiply the number of choices once for every level.
questions.onCorrect: Four levels of five choices reach 5^4 = 625 items, with only five choices to read on each screen.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 5 × 4. Each level multiplies the count by 5.
That is three levels. The menu has four.

questions.prompt: A shop has about 3,000 items and chooses 10 options per level. What is the smallest number of levels that can reach all of them?
hints: Compare 10 to the power of 3 with 3,000.
10^3 is 1,000, which is too few.
questions.onCorrect: Three levels reach only 1,000 items, and four levels reach 10,000, which covers 3,000 with room to spare.

misconceptions.feedback: Three levels of 10 reach 1,000 items, well short of 3,000.
Five levels reach 100,000. Four already cover 3,000.

questions.prompt: A menu has 6 choices per level over 3 levels. How many items can it reach?
hints: Multiply the number of choices once for each level.
questions.onCorrect: Three levels of six choices reach 6^3 = 216 items.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 6 × 3. Each level multiplies the count.
That is two levels. The menu has three.

questions.prompt: You have a proposed site structure and want to know whether people can find items in it. Which method?
hints: One method generates structures and another checks them.
The right method gives people findability tasks in a text-only hierarchy.
questions.onCorrect: A tree test sets findability tasks in the proposed hierarchy, so it measures whether the structure and labels work.

misconceptions.feedback: An open card sort generates ideas for a structure. It does not test one that already exists.
A colour test measures a visual choice, and the question concerns the hierarchy.
A closed card sort has participants place cards in categories that are already chosen. It checks whether items fit those categories, not whether people can find items.

questions.prompt: In a tree test, 14 of 20 participants reach the correct leaf. What is the success rate, as a percentage?
hints: Divide the number who succeeded by the number who tried.
questions.onCorrect: 14 of 20 is 0.7, which is a 70% success rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the proportion. The question asks for a percentage.
Six participants failed. Divide those who succeeded by the total.

questions.prompt: A team is testing its checkout. Which task is better written for a usability test?
hints: A good task gives a goal and a reason, and does not name the controls.
It also avoids asking for opinions.

acceptedIdeas: You have picked a jacket and want it delivered before Friday; buy it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: You have picked a jacket and want it delivered before Friday; buy it.

choices.label: You have picked a jacket and want it delivered before Friday; buy it.
Test the checkout from the basket to the confirmation page.
Use the Pay button on the cart page to complete the purchase.
Go through the checkout and tell us whether the page is clear.

questions.onCorrect: A scenario gives a goal in the user's own terms and leaves the route to them, so the test shows whether they can find the way.

misconceptions.feedback: The task names the control, so the test no longer shows whether the person can find it.
It asks for an opinion, and it gives no goal to act on.
It gives no goal, so each participant would invent a different task.

questions.prompt: During a test a participant says, "I'm looking for Delivery, and I'd expect it under Account." Asking participants for this running commentary is the ____-aloud protocol.
hints: The participant narrates a thought process.
questions.onCorrect: Speaking thoughts shows what a participant notices and expects, which is what the observer cannot see from the clicks alone.

questions.prompt: What percentage of problems do 3 users find, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Compute (1 − 0.25)^3 first.
Subtract from 1 and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Three users find about 58% and five find about 76%, so each added user finds fewer new problems than the one before.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share still missed, 0.75^3. Subtract it from 1.
That is 3 × 25%. Each user finds many of the same problems, so the shares do not add.

questions.prompt: Some problems are harder still to find, and L is only 0.10. What percentage do 5 users find, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Use 1 − (1 − L)^n with L = 0.10.
questions.onCorrect: With L = 0.10, five users find about 41%, so a product with subtle problems needs more rounds or more users.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result for L = 0.31. Here L is much smaller, so fewer problems are found.
That is the share missed, 0.9^5. Subtract it from 1.
That is 5 × 10%. The users find overlapping problems, so the shares do not add.

questions.prompt: A participant answers 3 on every item of the SUS. What is the score?
hints: An odd item contributes its response minus 1, and an even item contributes 5 minus its response.
Each item contributes 2, so the sum is 20.
Multiply the sum by 2.5.
questions.onCorrect: A neutral answer to every item scores 50, which is below the commonly quoted average of about 68.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum before multiplying by 2.5.
That multiplies the answers, 10 × 3. Each item first contributes response − 1 or 5 − response.

questions.prompt: With L = 0.4, what is the smallest number of users that finds at least 90% of the problems?
hints: Try n = 4 and n = 5 in 1 − 0.6^n.
Four users find about 87.0%, which is under 90%.
Five users find about 92.2%.
questions.onCorrect: Four users reach 87.0%, short of the mark, and five reach 92.2%, so five is the smallest number that gets to 90%.

misconceptions.feedback: Four users find 1 − 0.6^4 = 87.0%, which falls under 90%.
Three users find 1 − 0.6^3 = 78.4%, well short of 90%.

questions.prompt: With L = 0.2, what percentage of problems do 5 users find, to the nearest whole number?
hints: Subtract that from 1.
Convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Five users find about 67% when L is 0.2, well short of the 84% they find when L is 0.31.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share missed. Subtract 0.8^5 from 1.
That is 5 × 20%. The users find overlapping problems, so the shares do not add.

questions.prompt: A participant gives 5 to every odd-numbered SUS item and 2 to every even-numbered item. What is the SUS score?
hints: Odd items contribute response − 1, even items contribute 5 − response.
Each odd item contributes 4 and each even item 3, so the sum is 35.
Multiply by 2.5.
questions.onCorrect: The five odd items contribute 4 each and the five even items 3 each, so the sum is 35 and 35 × 2.5 = 87.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum before multiplying by 2.5.
That multiplies the sum of 35 by 2 and not by 2.5.

questions.prompt: Which task is better written for a usability test?
hints: Look for a goal that does not name the control.

acceptedIdeas: Your parcel is arriving on a day you will be away; get it delivered a day later.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Your parcel is arriving on a day you will be away; get it delivered a day later.

choices.label: Your parcel is arriving on a day you will be away; get it delivered a day later.
Click the 'Orders' tab and change the date.
Tell us if the date picker is clear.

questions.onCorrect: It gives a reason and a goal and leaves the participant to find the route.

misconceptions.feedback: It names the tab, so it tests whether people can follow directions.
It gives no goal, so participants would invent their own.
It asks for an opinion, and it gives nothing to do.

questions.prompt: Version B converts at 4.8% and version A at 4.0%, with 1,000 users each. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
hints: Ask how much a conversion rate would vary between two groups of 1,000 by chance alone.
A 0.8 point gap is small next to that variation.

acceptedIdeas: The data cannot yet distinguish the difference from chance
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The data cannot yet distinguish the difference from chance

choices.label: A and B are equal, since a gap under one point is too small to count
The result cannot be trusted until at least 10,000 users have seen each version
B is a clear winner, since 4.8 is 20% more than 4.0
The data cannot yet distinguish the difference from chance

questions.onCorrect: With only 1,000 users in each group, a gap of 0.8 points is within what chance produces, and the next screens show how to check this.

misconceptions.feedback: A 20% relative lift sounds large, but with 1,000 users each the rates vary by chance almost as much as the gap.
A gap that cannot be told from chance is not the same as no gap. The test cannot show that the versions differ, and it cannot show that they are equal either.
No fixed number of users makes a test valid. What matters is how large the gap is next to the chance variation at the sample size used.

questions.prompt: A team shows version B to every visitor who arrives on a Monday and version A to everyone else, so the two groups differ in more than the version. The groups should have been formed by ____ assignment.
hints: The assignment is made by chance and not by choice.
questions.onCorrect: Random assignment spreads every other difference between users across the groups evenly, so a difference in the metric can be attributed to the version.

questions.prompt: What is z for this difference and the standard error found above? Give it to two decimal places.
hints: z is the observed difference divided by its standard error.
0.010 divided by 0.00721.
The result is between 1 and 2.
questions.onCorrect: A z of 1.39 is still under 1.96, so even a full point of difference with 2,000 users each is not distinguishable from chance at the 95% level.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the standard error by the difference. z is the difference divided by the standard error.
That is the standard error. Divide the difference by it.

questions.prompt: The observed difference is 0.03 and its standard error is 0.012. What is z?
hints: Divide the difference by the standard error.
Compare the result with 1.96.
questions.onCorrect: A z of 2.5 exceeds 1.96, so the difference is significant at the 95% level.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 0.012 by 0.03. Divide the difference by the standard error.
That multiplies the two numbers. z is their ratio.

questions.prompt: An A/B test gives z = 2.4. At the 95% level, the difference is called statistically ____.
hints: The word describes a difference too large to attribute to chance.
questions.onCorrect: 2.4 is above 1.96, so chance alone would rarely produce a difference this large, which is a statement about evidence and not about whether the difference matters.

questions.prompt: Version A converts at 10.0% and B at 11.0%, with 5,000 users each. Work out z to two decimal places.
hints: The standard error is sqrt(p1(1 − p1)/n1 + p2(1 − p2)/n2).
The standard error is about 0.00613 and the difference is 0.01.
questions.onCorrect: A z of 1.63 is below 1.96, so even with 5,000 users each, a full point of difference is not significant at the 95% level.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the difference. z divides it by the standard error.
That is the threshold, not the z for these figures.

questions.prompt: If the standard error of the difference is 0.01 and the observed difference is 0.02, what is z?
hints: z is a ratio of the difference to its standard error.
Compare it with 1.96.
questions.onCorrect: z = 2 is just above 1.96, so this difference is significant at the 95% level.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the standard error by the difference. Divide the difference by the standard error.
That multiplies the two numbers. z is their ratio.

questions.prompt: Analytics show that 60% of users abandon at step 3. What can you conclude?
hints: Analytics record actions and not intentions.
questions.onCorrect: Analytics show what happened and where, and a reason has to come from watching or asking people.

misconceptions.feedback: A count of abandonments records the event and not the cause.
Length is one possible reason among many. The figures do not say which.
Nothing in a funnel count points to brand attitudes.

questions.prompt: A test finds a difference of 0.012 with a standard error of 0.008. What is z?
hints: Divide the difference by the standard error.
Compare with 1.96.
questions.onCorrect: z = 1.5 falls short of 1.96, so the difference is not significant at the 95% level.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the standard error by the difference. Divide the difference by the standard error.

questions.prompt: A file upload runs for twenty seconds, and for the whole of that time the screen shows a spinner and nothing else. What is the user missing?
hints: Think about what the user wonders after ten seconds of spinning.
The problem lies during the wait, not before or after it.

acceptedIdeas: Word of what the system is doing and how long it will take
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Word of what the system is doing and how long it will take

questions.onCorrect: Twenty seconds with only a spinner leaves the user unable to tell whether the upload is progressing or stuck, which is a failure of visibility of system status.

misconceptions.feedback: Undo matters after an action, but the trouble here comes while the upload runs, when the user cannot tell whether anything is happening.
A confirmation guards against starting by mistake. The trouble here comes after the upload has begun, when the user cannot tell whether anything is happening.

choices.label: A way to undo the upload once it has finished
A confirmation message before the upload starts
Word of what the system is doing and how long it will take

questions.prompt: A six-step setup wizard has no Back button, so a mistake on step two means starting again from the beginning. Which heuristic does this break?
hints: Think about a user who chose the wrong option on step two.
questions.onCorrect: Users need a clearly marked way out of a choice they did not mean, such as back or cancel, and this wizard offers none.

misconceptions.feedback: The wizard shows which step the user is on. The fault is that the user has no way back to an earlier one.
Nothing here differs from one page to another or from the platform's conventions. The trouble is the missing exit.
The screens are not cluttered. The problem is that a mistaken choice cannot be reversed.

questions.prompt: On one page of a site the main button is blue and labelled Save, and on another page it is grey and labelled Submit. Which heuristic does this break?
hints: Compare the two pages: is the same action presented the same way?
questions.onCorrect: The same action should look and read the same everywhere, so that users need not wonder whether different styles mean different things.

misconceptions.feedback: Save and Submit are both ordinary words a user knows. The fault is that the same action looks and reads differently on two pages.
Both buttons are on screen, so nothing has to be remembered. The fault is that the user has to wonder whether they mean the same thing.
That heuristic concerns shortcuts for experts. Here every user meets two styles for one action.

choices.label: Match between system and the real world

questions.prompt: The message 'NullReferenceException in FormHandler' gives no plain words and no way forward. Besides matching the real world, which heuristic names the need for a plain statement of the problem and a fix?
hints: It is the heuristic about error messages themselves.
Its name has three verbs.

acceptedIdeas: help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors
acceptedAlternatives: help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors
help users recognise diagnose and recover from errors
recognize, diagnose and recover from errors
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors.

questions.onCorrect: An error message should say in plain language what went wrong and offer a way forward, which this heuristic requires and a programmer's exception name does not.

questions.prompt: A checkout asks the user to type a long product code that was printed on an earlier page, and the earlier page is no longer visible. Which heuristic does this break?
hints: Ask where the code is while the user types it.
questions.onCorrect: The checkout makes the user hold the code in memory, where showing it beside the box would let them simply read it.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing here varies from page to page. The fault is that the user must carry the code in memory across a page change.
Documentation would not help, because the code is specific to this order and has gone from the screen.
The screen is not crowded. The difficulty is that information the user needs is no longer on it.

questions.prompt: A settings page shows forty options with equal weight, and the one the user needs is lost among rarely used ones. Which heuristic does this break?
hints: Ask whether all forty options need to be shown with the same weight.
questions.onCorrect: Every rarely needed option competes with the needed one and lowers its visibility, which is what minimalist design guards against.

misconceptions.feedback: Every option is visible, so nothing has to be recalled. The cost is scanning past the ones that are rarely needed.
That heuristic concerns accelerators for expert users. Here every user has to search a crowded page.
Help would explain the options, but the trouble is that rarely used ones compete with the one the user needs.

questions.prompt: How many heuristics are in Nielsen's list?
hints: The list is sometimes called the ten usability heuristics.
Count the headings in the two lists.
The number is in the name.
questions.onCorrect: Nielsen refined the list to ten heuristics in 1994, and it is still the version in common use.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of chunks people are sometimes said to remember. The list has ten items.
Five is the length of one of the two figure lists. The list has ten.

questions.prompt: What is a usability heuristic?
hints: Think about whether two evaluators could disagree about whether a heuristic is met.

acceptedIdeas: A broad rule of thumb that prompts questions about a design
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A broad rule of thumb that prompts questions about a design

questions.onCorrect: Because the rules are broad, one problem can break several of them, and the evaluator records the one that explains it best.

misconceptions.feedback: A heuristic is deliberately broad. It says what a good interface tends to do and leaves the evaluator to judge whether a given screen does it.
Measurements come from testing with users. A heuristic is applied by an evaluator looking at the interface, with no users present.

choices.label: A measurement taken while users carry out a task
A precise rule that a design either passes or fails
A broad rule of thumb that prompts questions about a design

questions.prompt: A form deletes a record immediately with no undo. Which heuristic does this violate?
hints: Think about how the user can recover from an action they did not mean.
questions.onCorrect: Users need a way out of unwanted actions, such as undo or cancel.

misconceptions.feedback: The screen is not cluttered. The problem is that the action cannot be reversed.
A manual would not help someone who has already lost the record.
Nothing in the screen is inconsistent. The trouble is that no exit exists.

questions.prompt: A spinner runs for 20 seconds with no message. Which heuristic?
hints: The user cannot tell what the system is doing.
questions.onCorrect: Visibility of system status asks the system to keep users informed about what is going on, with feedback in reasonable time.

misconceptions.feedback: No error has occurred or been prevented here. The user simply cannot see what is happening.
Shortcuts for experts are not the issue. Every user is left without information.
The user is not asked to remember anything. The system just says nothing.

questions.prompt: Each of two evaluators independently finds 35% of an interface's problems. Roughly what share do they find between them?
hints: Ask what happens to a problem that both evaluators find.
The two lists overlap.

acceptedIdeas: Somewhat less than 70%, since their finds overlap
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Somewhat less than 70%, since their finds overlap

questions.onCorrect: Some problems are found by both, so the share is below the sum; the next screens show how to calculate it as about 57.8%.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding the shares counts twice every problem that both evaluators find, and working independently they will overlap on some.
Independent evaluators find different problems as well as some of the same ones, so together they find more than either alone.
They work alone, so neither prompts the other, and the overlap between their finds pulls the total below the sum.

choices.label: 35%, since they find the same problems
Somewhat less than 70%, since their finds overlap
Exactly 70%, since the two shares add
More than 70%, since each prompts the other

questions.prompt: Two evaluators read each other's notes before they start, and their lists then overlap far more than usual. How should the first pass have been done?
hints: Think about what makes the evaluators' findings differ.
The merge comes after the first pass.

acceptedIdeas: Each evaluator alone, with the lists merged afterwards
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each evaluator alone, with the lists merged afterwards

questions.onCorrect: Independent passes keep each evaluator's view intact, and the merge then shows where the views differ, which is what makes it useful.

misconceptions.feedback: Working together makes the lists overlap even more, since each evaluator is steered by what the other has already seen.
One evaluator finds only around a third of the problems, and a second working alone finds others, so a single pass loses what the extra evaluator would add.
Agreeing the problems in advance pushes the evaluators towards the same findings, and the value of several evaluators lies in the problems they do not share.

choices.label: Both evaluators together, so that each can check the other's findings
Each evaluator alone, with the lists merged afterwards
One evaluator doing the whole pass, since a single list avoids duplicates
Against a shared list of problems agreed in advance

questions.prompt: What share of the problems do 4 evaluators find, to one decimal place?
hints: Subtract from 1 and convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Four evaluators find about 76.0%, only 10.3 points more than three, so the gain from each added evaluator is shrinking.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share missed by all four. Subtract it from 1.
That adds 4 × 30%. Overlap means shares do not add.

questions.prompt: A Submit button that does nothing on phones stops most users from sending the sign-up form. What rating should it get on Nielsen's 0 to 4 severity scale?
hints: Ask how many users meet it and whether they can get past it.
The top of the scale is for problems that must be fixed before release.
questions.onCorrect: It is frequent, it cannot be overcome and it blocks the main task, so it rates 4, a catastrophe to fix before release.

misconceptions.feedback: A minor problem slows users down. This one stops most of them from finishing at all.
A cosmetic problem is fixed only if time allows, and a form that cannot be sent is far more than cosmetic.
A major problem is important to fix, but one that stops most users from completing the main task belongs at the top of the scale.

questions.prompt: How many questions does a cognitive walkthrough ask at each action?
hints: The questions run from trying the action to seeing progress.
Try, notice, connect, see progress.
Count them.
questions.onCorrect: The four questions are whether the user will try the right effect, notice the action, connect it to the goal and see progress.

misconceptions.feedback: Three leaves out one of the steps: try, notice, connect, and see progress.
Ten is the number of heuristics. A walkthrough asks four questions at each action.

questions.prompt: A cognitive walkthrough steps through one task and stops at every action the interface requires. What does the evaluator ask at each action?
hints: The method is about how easily a new user can learn the interface.

acceptedIdeas: Whether a new user would find the right action and see it work
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether a new user would find the right action and see it work

questions.onCorrect: The first three questions concern execution and the fourth concerns evaluation, the two gulfs met in the lesson on mental models.

misconceptions.feedback: Checking a screen against the heuristics is a heuristic evaluation. A walkthrough follows one task and asks how a new user would fare at each step.
Severity is rated after problems have been found, in either method. The walkthrough's questions are about whether a new user would find the way.
A walkthrough is about learning, so it asks about a first-time user, and it does not time anyone.

choices.label: How long an expert would take to complete the action
How severe each problem is on the 0 to 4 scale
Whether a new user would find the right action and see it work
Which of the ten heuristics the screen breaks

questions.prompt: Suppose each evaluator finds only 20% of the problems, independently. What is the smallest number of evaluators who together find at least 75%?
hints: The share found is 1 − 0.8^n.
Try n = 6, where 0.8^6 is about 0.262.
Six find about 73.8%, so test n = 7.
questions.onCorrect: Six evaluators reach 73.8% and seven reach 79.0%, so seven are needed, which shows why a weaker evaluator pool costs more people.

misconceptions.feedback: Six evaluators find 73.8%, just under 75%.
Four find 59.0%, well short of 75%.

questions.prompt: If each evaluator independently finds 40% of problems, what percentage do 3 find together, to one decimal place?
hints: Subtract that from 1.
Convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Three evaluators find about 78.4%, a little less than twice what one finds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share missed by all three. Subtract it from 1.
That adds 3 × 40%. Evaluators overlap, so the shares do not add.

questions.prompt: A problem that stops users from completing checkout. On Nielsen's 0 to 4 scale, it is:
hints: Consider frequency, impact and persistence.
A blocked checkout has the highest possible impact.
questions.onCorrect: Users cannot complete the main task, so the impact is severe, and the problem is rated a major problem or a catastrophe.

misconceptions.feedback: A 0 means it is not a problem at all, and a blocked checkout is a serious one.
A 2 is a minor problem, low priority. A problem that blocks checkout prevents the main goal.
A 1 is cosmetic, fixed only if time allows.

questions.prompt: You have no users available this week and only a mock-up. Which method fits?
hints: Which method needs no participants?
questions.onCorrect: A heuristic evaluation is done by evaluators against a set of rules, so it can run on a mock-up without users.

misconceptions.feedback: An A/B test needs live traffic and a built product.
A survey needs respondents, and a mock-up cannot be rated by an audience that is not available.
A tree test needs participants to attempt tasks.

questions.prompt: A date field offers a calendar picker that shows only real dates. What happens to the error of entering 31 February?
hints: Ask whether 31 February appears anywhere in the picker.

acceptedIdeas: It can no longer happen at all
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It can no longer happen at all

questions.onCorrect: A control that offers only valid values removes the error altogether, which is better than any message about it.

misconceptions.feedback: A picker of real dates has no 31 February to choose, so there is nothing for a message to report.
Care has nothing to do with it. The date is simply not among the options, so no amount of carelessness can produce it.

choices.label: It can no longer happen at all
It happens less often, since users take more care with a picker
It still happens, but the message about it is clearer

questions.prompt: A quantity field offers only a dropdown of the numbers 1 to 10, so nobody can enter a letter or a negative number. A design that limits the options in this way is a ____.
hints: The lesson on mental models used this word for something that limits the options, such as a plug that fits one way only.
questions.onCorrect: A constraint stops the wrong action from being available, which is the strongest form of error prevention.

questions.prompt: How many of the three parts of a good message does "Invalid input." supply?
hints: Read the message and ask what it tells the user about the field.
It does not say which field, what is wrong or how to fix it.
Count the parts it supplies.
questions.onCorrect: The message names no field, gives no cause and offers no step, so it supplies none of the three parts.

misconceptions.feedback: 'Invalid' does not even say which field or what is wrong, so it does not supply the first part.
The message has two words and supplies none of the three parts.

questions.prompt: A card number field has received a number with one digit missing. Which message follows good error-message practice?
hints: A good message says what happened and why, in the user's words.
Which one gives the user a number to work with?

acceptedIdeas: The card number needs 16 digits and you entered 15.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The card number needs 16 digits and you entered 15.

choices.label: Something went wrong, so please try the form again.
Error 400: the request could not be processed.
The card number needs 16 digits and you entered 15.
The card number you entered is not valid.

questions.onCorrect: It says what is wrong with the card number and why, and the user can see what to do next.

misconceptions.feedback: It says that the number is wrong, and nothing about why or what to change.
A code is a term from the system and not from the user's language.
It gives no cause and no step, and it does not even say which field is at fault.

questions.prompt: After a user archives an email, a bar appears for a few seconds with a button that brings the email back. The button lets the user ____ the action.
hints: It is the opposite of doing the action, in one word.
questions.onCorrect: Undo costs nothing when the action was intended, whereas a confirmation costs every user a click on every action.

misconceptions.feedback: Confirmation asks before the action. The question describes reversing it afterwards.

questions.prompt: A sign-up form shows grey text saying Email inside the field, and it disappears as soon as typing begins. To keep the field's name on screen and announced by a screen reader, the form needs a ____ element.
hints: An in-field hint disappears when typing begins, and this element does not.
questions.onCorrect: A label stays on screen and gives the field its accessible name, and clicking it moves focus to the field.

misconceptions.feedback: An in-field hint disappears when the user types and is not a reliable name for the field.

questions.prompt: A form pre-selects the country the user is most likely to live in, so that most users need not choose. A value supplied in this way is a ____.
hints: It is the value the form uses unless the user changes it.
questions.onCorrect: A sensible default removes work and removes the chance of an error for the many users who would choose the same value.

questions.prompt: A good error message says what happened, why it happened and what to do next. How many things must it say?
hints: Count the questions the message must answer.
What happened, why, and what next.
The list has as many items as the sentence names.
questions.onCorrect: Three, and the message should also use the user's words and sit next to the field concerned.

misconceptions.feedback: The message must also say what to do next, a third thing.
The three parts are what happened, why and what next. Position and wording are separate rules.

questions.prompt: A phone number field rejects a value. Which message gives all three parts of a good error message?
hints: A good message says what happened, why, and what to do next.

acceptedIdeas: The phone number is too short: it needs 11 digits and has 10. Check for a missing digit.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The phone number is too short: it needs 11 digits and has 10. Check for a missing digit.

questions.onCorrect: It says what happened, why, and what to do next, in the user's words, and it belongs beside the phone field.

misconceptions.feedback: It says what happened, but not why the number was rejected or what to do about it.
It names no field and gives no cause, so the user has to find the problem unaided.

choices.label: Please check the form, because something in it was not accepted, and try again.
The phone number is too short: it needs 11 digits and has 10. Check for a missing digit.
The phone number is not valid, so the form could not be sent.

questions.prompt: Checking a field's value as the user leaves it, before the form is submitted, is called inline ____.
hints: The field is checked for being valid.
questions.onCorrect: Inline validation after the user leaves a field avoids a wall of errors at the end, and it should not fire while the user is still typing.

questions.prompt: In `<input type="email" required>`, which two things does the browser check before submitting?
hints: Think about what `required` and `type="email"` each say.
A browser checks the shape of a value, not whether an address is real.

acceptedIdeas: That the field is not empty and that its value looks like an email address
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the field is not empty and that its value looks like an email address

choices.label: That the user has an account and that the value has an @
That the field is not empty and that its value looks like an email address
That the field is on screen and not hidden
That the email address exists and that the field is not empty

questions.onCorrect: `required` makes the browser reject an empty field and `type="email"` makes it check that the value looks like an address.

misconceptions.feedback: A browser cannot tell whether an address exists. It checks only that the value looks like one.
The browser knows nothing about accounts. It checks the shape of the value.
Visibility is not part of these attributes.

questions.prompt: Which statement about who benefits from accessible design is most accurate?
hints: Think of a bright sun on a phone screen, or a broken arm.
A limit can be short-lived or tied to the setting.

acceptedIdeas: People with permanent, temporary and situational limits all benefit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: People with permanent, temporary and situational limits all benefit

choices.label: Only people with permanent disabilities benefit
It matters mainly to the few who use screen readers
People with permanent, temporary and situational limits all benefit

questions.onCorrect: Glare, a broken arm and a noisy room give anyone a temporary or situational limit, so accessible design helps far more people than those with a permanent disability.

misconceptions.feedback: Temporary limits such as a broken arm and situational ones such as glare affect everyone at times.
Age is one factor among many. Limits can arise at any age.
Screen reader users are one group among many, and contrast, captions and large targets help others.

questions.prompt: Criterion 2.1.1 requires that all functionality be available from a keyboard. Which POUR principle does it fall under?
hints: Ask whether the criterion is about sensing, working, following or interpreting the page.
questions.onCorrect: Keyboard access is about whether users can work the interface, which is the Operable principle.

misconceptions.feedback: Perceivable concerns whether users can sense the content, as with contrast and text alternatives. Keyboard use is about working the controls.
Understandable concerns whether users can follow the content and its behaviour, as with error messages. Reaching a control by keyboard comes before that.
Robust concerns whether browsers and assistive technologies can interpret the content, as with name, role and value.

questions.prompt: What is the contrast ratio for L1 = 0.8 and L2 = 0.2? Give a single number, to one decimal place.
hints: Add 0.05 to each luminance.
The numerator is 0.85 and the denominator is 0.25.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: A ratio of 3.4 is below the 4.5 needed for normal text, though it passes for large text.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 0.8 by 0.2. Add 0.05 to each luminance first.
That divides the darker value by the lighter. The lighter goes on top.

questions.prompt: Black has relative luminance 0, and a pale yellow has 0.75. What is the contrast ratio of black text on that yellow? Give a single number.
hints: Add 0.05 to each luminance.
The numerator is 0.80 and the denominator is 0.05.
Divide 0.80 by 0.05.
questions.onCorrect: Black on a light colour gives a high ratio, though it stays below the 21 of black on white, the largest the formula can give.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 0.75 by 0.05 without adding 0.05 to the lighter colour.
That would be two identical colours. Black and a pale yellow are far apart.

questions.prompt: A heading is set in 24 point regular type. At level AA, what is the smallest contrast ratio it needs?
hints: Check whether 24 point counts as large text.
Large text is 18 point or more, so the lower requirement applies.
questions.onCorrect: Large text is 18 point or more, or 14 point bold or more, so a 24 point heading needs 3:1 at AA.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure for normal text. At 24 point the heading is large text, which needs less.
That is the stricter AAA figure for normal text.

questions.prompt: A button's border has relative luminance 0.3 against a white background of 1. What is the contrast ratio? Give a single number, to one decimal place.
hints: Add 0.05 to each luminance.
The numerator is 1.05 and the denominator is 0.35.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The ratio is exactly 3:1, which just meets the requirement for key interface components under criterion 1.4.11.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 1 by 0.3. Add 0.05 to each luminance first.
That divides the darker value by the lighter. The lighter goes on top.

questions.prompt: Two colours have relative luminance 0.7 and 0.1. What is the contrast ratio, (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05)? Give a single number.
hints: Add 0.05 to each luminance.
The numerator is 0.75 and the denominator is 0.15.
Divide the first by the second.
questions.onCorrect: 0.75 divided by 0.15 is 5.0, which passes AA for normal text.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 0.7 by 0.1. Add 0.05 to each luminance first.
That divides the darker value by the lighter. The lighter goes on top.

questions.prompt: Normal-size text has a contrast ratio of 4.48:1. Does it meet WCAG 2.2 AA (1.4.3)?
hints: Compare 4.48 with 4.5.
The computed value is compared exactly with the requirement.

acceptedIdeas: No, it falls short of AA
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, it falls short of AA

choices.label: No, it falls short of AA

questions.onCorrect: 4.48 is just under 4.5 and the ratio is compared exactly, so the pair falls short; #777777 on white is such a pair, while #767676 reaches 4.54.

misconceptions.feedback: The requirement is at least 4.5, and a ratio below that line cannot be rounded up to reach it.
Bold helps only when the text is also at least 14 point, which would make it large text with a lower requirement. This text is normal size.
The criterion does not depend on the device.

questions.prompt: In POUR, the R stands for ____.
hints: It is about content working with different browsers and assistive technologies.
questions.onCorrect: Robust content can be interpreted reliably by a wide range of user agents, including assistive technologies.

questions.prompt:
A page has these five controls in a row. Which of them can a keyboard user reach with the Tab key, with no extra code? `Home
Menu
Next`
hints: Links, buttons and form fields are focusable by default.
A div or span with only a click handler is not focusable.

acceptedIdeas: The link, the button and the text field
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The link, the button and the text field

questions.onCorrect: The link, the button and the text field are focusable, while the div and the span are not, so a keyboard user cannot reach Menu or Next.

misconceptions.feedback: A click handler makes a div or a span respond to a mouse, but it does not put the element in the Tab order.
A link with an href is a native interactive element, so it is in the Tab order as well.
Native links, buttons and form fields are in the Tab order by default, with no script needed.

choices.label: None, until a script adds them to the Tab order
Only the button and the text field
All five, since each one responds to a click
The link, the button and the text field

questions.prompt: The native element that is focusable and can be activated with both Enter and Space is the ____ element.
hints: It is the element for an action such as Save.
questions.onCorrect: A button comes with focus, a role and keyboard activation, which a div must have added by hand.

misconceptions.feedback: A div or span has none of these behaviours until they are added with extra code.

questions.prompt: Which element should the Delivery information control use?
hints: Ask whether the control does something on this page or takes the user to another one.
Navigation and action use different elements.
questions.onCorrect: A link, the `a` element with an `href`, is announced as a link and can be opened in a new tab, which a button cannot do.

misconceptions.feedback: A button performs an action on the page. This control takes the user to another page, and that is navigation.
A div has no focus, role or keyboard behaviour unless they are all added by hand, and a real element already supplies them.

questions.prompt: A blurred photo of an office sits behind a page header only to soften it, and it carries no information. Its img element should have an ____ alt attribute.
hints: It is present but has nothing between its quotation marks.
questions.onCorrect: An empty alt tells a screen reader to ignore the image, whereas a missing alt often makes it read out the file name.

misconceptions.feedback: Words in the alt would be read aloud. A decorative image gets an attribute with nothing in it.

questions.prompt: An icon button is 20 × 20 CSS px, and no spacing exception applies. By how many CSS px is its width short of the AA minimum?
hints: The AA minimum comes from the target size criterion that is new in WCAG 2.2.
Subtract the button's width from the minimum.
24 minus 20.
questions.onCorrect: The width is 20 and the minimum is 24, so the button is 4 CSS px short in each direction.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the minimum itself. The question asks for how far the button falls short.
That is the AAA size, and the question asks about the AA minimum.

questions.prompt: An icon button is 22 × 22 CSS px, and other targets sit close enough that the spacing exception does not apply. Does it meet criterion 2.5.8 at level AA?
hints: Compare the button with the AA minimum of 24 by 24 CSS px.

acceptedIdeas: No, since it is smaller than 24 by 24 CSS px
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since it is smaller than 24 by 24 CSS px

questions.onCorrect: At 22 px it is 2 px short of the 24 px minimum in each direction, and with no room for the spacing exception it fails.

misconceptions.feedback: WCAG's thresholds are exact, so a target 2 px short of the minimum fails just as one 10 px short does.
The AA minimum in criterion 2.5.8 is 24 by 24 CSS px, so a 22 px button falls short of it, although it is larger than 20.

choices.label: Yes, since the AA minimum is 20 by 20 CSS px
No, since it is smaller than 24 by 24 CSS px
Yes, since 22 px is close enough to the minimum

questions.prompt:
Which elements in this snippet have an accessibility problem? `
Save
Help Next`
hints: Look for an image with no alt, controls that are not native, and a field with no label.
The button and the link are native elements with text.

acceptedIdeas: The img, the div, the input and the span
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The img, the div, the input and the span

questions.onCorrect: The image has no alt, the field has no label, and the div and the span cannot be reached from a keyboard, which makes four problems.

misconceptions.feedback: The div and the span cannot be reached from a keyboard, but the image also has no alt attribute and the text field has no label.
The text field has an id but nothing points to it, so it has no label for a screen reader to announce.
The button and the link are native elements with visible text, so they are focusable and named.

choices.label: The img, the div, the input and the span
Only the div and the span
The img, the div and the span

questions.prompt: Which element is focusable and operable by Enter and Space by default?
hints: Native controls come with keyboard behaviour built in.
questions.onCorrect: A button is focusable and responds to Enter and Space with no extra code, and it announces itself as a button.

misconceptions.feedback: A div is not focusable unless tabindex and key handlers are added.
A span is not focusable by default either.
A paragraph is text and not a control.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum target size under WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.5.8 at level AA?
hints: The criterion is new in WCAG 2.2.
It is smaller than the size asked for by the enhanced criterion.
questions.onCorrect: Pointer targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, unless an exception such as spacing applies.

misconceptions.feedback: A target of 20 px can pass only through the spacing exception, and it is not the minimum size itself.
WCAG sets no 32 px threshold. The AA minimum is smaller than that.
That is the enhanced size in criterion 2.5.5 at level AAA. The AA minimum is smaller.

questions.prompt: A purely decorative swirl behind a page title should have which alt attribute?
hints: A screen reader should skip it entirely.
questions.onCorrect: An empty alt tells assistive technology to skip a decorative image.

misconceptions.feedback: The word would be read aloud and add noise.
That would announce a meaningless word.
Leaving the text out altogether can make some screen readers read the file name.

questions.prompt: After the change, by how many px is the label nearer to its own field than to the field above it?
hints: The label is now 4 px from its own field.
The field above it is now 24 px away.
Subtract the smaller gap from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: The label is 4 px from its own field and 24 px from the field above, a difference of 20 px in favour of the field it names.

misconceptions.feedback: 4 px is the gap to its own field. The question asks how much nearer that is than the gap to the field above.
24 px is the gap to the field above. Subtract the gap to its own field from it.
Adding the gaps gives 28 px. The question asks for the difference.
16 px was the difference before the change, with gaps of 8 px and 24 px. After it the gaps are 4 px and 24 px.

questions.prompt: A toolbar button is moved from the very top edge of the screen to a position 60 px below it, with the same drawn size, so the pointer can now travel past it. What happens to the button's index of difficulty?
hints: Ask what the pointer does when it reaches the edge of the screen, and what it does 60 px away from it.
Width in Fitts's law is the size of the target along the line of movement.

acceptedIdeas: It rises, because the pointer can overshoot, so the width along the movement is no longer unlimited
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises, because the pointer can overshoot, so the width along the movement is no longer unlimited

questions.onCorrect: Away from the edge a pointer that goes too far lands beyond the button, so the width counts only as drawn and the index of difficulty rises.

choices.label: It stays the same, because the button's drawn size and its distance from the pointer are unchanged
It falls, because a button that stands clear of the edge is easier to notice and aim at
It rises, because the pointer can overshoot, so the width along the movement is no longer unlimited
