misconceptions.feedback: The drawn size is not what counts at the edge. There the pointer stops, so the width along the movement is effectively unlimited, and moving the button away takes that advantage with it.
Fitts's law measures the movement, and not how easily the button is noticed. What changes when the button leaves the edge is what happens to a pointer that goes too far.

questions.prompt: A team wants to understand how people choose a restaurant on its booking app, and plans to ask a few of them. Which question is most likely to give reliable evidence?
hints: The step before explained which kind of question returns an event.
Compare questions about the past with questions about wishes and the future.

acceptedIdeas: Walk me through the last time you picked a restaurant on the app.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Walk me through the last time you picked a restaurant on the app.

questions.onCorrect: A question about a specific past event returns what actually happened, which is firmer evidence than a wish, a forecast or a rating.

choices.label: Which new features would you like us to add to the booking app?
How often do you think you will use the new booking page next month?
Do you find booking a table through the app easy to do?
Walk me through the last time you picked a restaurant on the app.

misconceptions.feedback: A request for wishes asks people to design a solution, and what they say they want is a guess about what they would use.
A forecast of future use runs into the say-do gap, since what people expect to do often differs from what they then do.
A rating of how easy something is asks for a summary judgement, which people shape to what they think is expected. It does not describe an event.

questions.prompt: A team is testing the renewal feature of a library app. Which task is better written for a usability test?
hints: Look for a goal that does not name the control.

acceptedIdeas: Your book is due back on Friday and you will be abroad; keep it for another week.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Your book is due back on Friday and you will be abroad; keep it for another week.

questions.onCorrect: It gives a reason and a goal and leaves the participant to find the route.

choices.label: Open the Loans page, choose your book and press Renew.
Your book is due back on Friday and you will be abroad; keep it for another week.
Test the renewal feature and note anything that seems wrong.
Open the Loans page and tell us whether the Renew button is easy to find.

misconceptions.feedback: The task names the page and the button, so the test shows only whether people can follow directions and not whether they can find the way.
It gives no goal, so each participant would invent a different task.
It asks for an opinion and names the control, and it gives the participant nothing to achieve.

questions.prompt: A page shows "Something went wrong. Please try again." for every failure, whatever the cause. The words are plain and polite, but the message never says what failed or what the user could do differently. Which heuristic explains the problem best?
hints: Ask which heuristic is about what an error message has to contain.
The message is in plain words, so one of the heuristics is already met.

acceptedIdeas: Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors

questions.onCorrect: An error message should say in plain words what went wrong and suggest a way forward, and this one does neither, which is what the error heuristic asks for.

choices.label: Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors
Match between system and the real world

misconceptions.feedback: The words are ordinary and the user understands them. The fault is in what the message leaves out.
The user is told that something failed, so the status is not hidden. What is missing is an explanation of the failure and a way forward, which another heuristic covers.
Documentation is a separate resource that the user has to go and find. The explanation here belongs in the message itself, at the moment of the failure.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet user applies the same five-step filter hundreds of times a day, and the app offers no shortcut, saved filter or way to repeat the steps. Which heuristic does this break?
hints: Think about the difference between what a novice and an expert need.
questions.onCorrect: Experts need accelerators such as shortcuts and saved settings, and an app that offers none makes them repeat every step by hand.

misconceptions.feedback: Every control is visible, so nothing has to be remembered. The cost is the repeated effort for a user who already knows the steps.
No error is described here. The trouble is the time an expert spends repeating steps.
Nothing differs from page to page or from the platform's conventions. The cost comes from repetition.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy app lists an order as "Rx adjudication pending", and customers do not know what the words mean. Which heuristic does this break?
hints: The line does give the user some information. Ask whose words it is written in.

acceptedIdeas: Match between system and the real world
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Match between system and the real world

questions.onCorrect: The system should speak the user's language, with words the customer knows and not terms from inside the business.

choices.label: Match between system and the real world

misconceptions.feedback: The line does report a status, so the user is kept informed. The fault is that the words belong to the pharmacy and not to the customer.
The line adds no clutter. It uses a term from inside the pharmacy business.
Documentation would explain the term after the customer went looking for it. The better repair is to use words the customer already knows.

questions.prompt: Every new user meets a set-up screen that blocks the whole app for ten minutes, and nobody ever sees that screen again after the first time. Of the three factors in a severity rating, which one is low for this problem?
hints: Ask which factor depends on whether the problem catches the same user again and again.
questions.onCorrect: Persistence asks whether users are caught every time or only once, and a screen met a single time scores low on it however hard that one time is.

misconceptions.feedback: A ten-minute block is hard to get past, so the impact is high.
Every new user meets the screen, so the problem reaches many users.

questions.prompt: A team has a mock-up of the set-up screens in a new thermostat app and wants to find where a first-time user would go wrong at each step of one task. Which method fits?
hints: The method follows one task and asks questions at each action.
questions.onCorrect: A cognitive walkthrough takes one task and asks at each action whether a first-time user would try the right effect, notice the action, connect it and see progress.

misconceptions.feedback: A heuristic evaluation looks at whole screens and asks which of the ten rules they break. It does not follow one task step by step as a new user would.
An A/B test compares two live versions on real traffic, and a mock-up cannot supply that.
A tree test checks where people go in a hierarchy of labels. It does not follow a task through a set of screens.

questions.prompt: Bold text at 14 point has a contrast ratio of 3.2 to 1 against its background. Does it meet WCAG 2.2 level AA for contrast (1.4.3)?
hints: Decide first whether the text counts as large.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because 14 point bold counts as large text, which needs 3 to 1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because 14 point bold counts as large text, which needs 3 to 1

questions.onCorrect: Large text is 18 point or more, or 14 point bold or more, and it needs only 3 to 1, so a ratio of 3.2 passes.

choices.label: No, because text needs at least 4.5 to 1 and this is below it
No, because bold text needs a higher ratio than regular text
Yes, because 14 point bold counts as large text, which needs 3 to 1
Yes, because any ratio above 3 to 1 passes for text of every size

misconceptions.feedback: The 4.5 to 1 requirement is for normal text. Text that is 14 point bold or larger counts as large and has a lower requirement.
Bold does not raise the requirement. At 14 point it moves the text into the large category, which has the lower one.
The lower requirement applies only to large text, so for normal-size text 3 to 1 would not be enough.

flashcards.front: Grouping by nearness: elements with small gaps between them read as one unit. What is the cue called?
flashcards.back: Proximity compares gaps, so the smaller gap joins elements and the larger gap separates them.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Proximity compares gaps, so the smaller gap joins elements and the larger gap separates them.

flashcards.front: Why is a divider line often unnecessary between two groups on a page?
flashcards.back: A wider gap already separates the groups, so the line adds a second mark for the eye to process.

flashcards.front: Six dots have gaps of 8, 8, 40, 8 and 8 px. How many groups does the viewer see?
flashcards.back: The 40 px gap is the only boundary, so the row reads as two groups of three.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 40 px gap is the only boundary, so the row reads as two groups of three.

flashcards.front: The small store holding the items a person is using right now is called ____ memory.
flashcards.back: Working memory holds roughly four chunks at once, so designs should not rely on users carrying more.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Working memory holds roughly four chunks at once, so designs should not rely on users carrying more.

flashcards.front: A reference is shown as 4 5 7 1 grouped as 45 71. How many chunks?
flashcards.back: The two groups are held as two chunks.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two groups are held as two chunks.

flashcards.front: Why does a screen that shows the previous choice help more than one that asks the user to remember it?
flashcards.back: Showing it turns recall into recognition and spares the limited working memory for the task.

flashcards.front: A target is 3 cm wide and 9 cm away. What is ID in bits?
flashcards.back: D/W = 3, so ID = log2(4) = 2 bits.

flashcards.front: Fitts's law uses the target's size along the line of motion. What symbol is this size given?
flashcards.back: W is the width of the target along the direction of movement, and D is the distance to it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: W is the width of the target along the direction of movement, and D is the distance to it.

flashcards.front: Hick's law says time grows as log2(n + 1). Why does that not mean fewer items is always better?
flashcards.back: The time grows slowly with n, so a well-organised long list can beat a deep tree of menus, and the law assumes equally likely options.

flashcards.front: The designer's model reaches the user only through the ____ image.
flashcards.back: The system image is everything the user can see and do, so it has to carry the designer's model.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The system image is everything the user can see and do, so it has to carry the designer's model.

flashcards.front: The gap between what a user wants to do and the actions the system shows is the gulf of ____.
flashcards.back: Execution is about finding and performing the action, and evaluation is about reading the result.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Execution is about finding and performing the action, and evaluation is about reading the result.

flashcards.front: Why is a mental model allowed to differ from how a system is built?
flashcards.back: People form working pictures from what they see, and these can be useful and still wrong, so the design has to show the real behaviour.

flashcards.front: A survey of n = 100 has p = 0.5. What is the 95% margin in percentage points, to one decimal place?
A question that suggests the answer wanted is called a ____ question.
flashcards.back: Leading wording turns an answer into agreement, so rewrite it to ask about a specific past event.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leading wording turns an answer into agreement, so rewrite it to ask about a specific past event.

flashcards.front: Why should an interview ask about past behaviour and not about the features users want?
flashcards.back: People describe what they did reliably and propose solutions poorly, so a past event gives evidence and a wish gives a guess.

flashcards.front: A menu has 5 choices per level over 3 levels. How many items can it reach?
The method that gives participants a text-only hierarchy and tasks to find items is a ____ test.
flashcards.back: A tree test measures success and directness on the proposed structure and labels.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tree test measures success and directness on the proposed structure and labels.

flashcards.front: Why does a card sort not test a navigation?
flashcards.back: It shows how people group items, which gives ideas for a structure, and only a tree test measures whether a structure lets them find things.

flashcards.front: L = 0.31. About what percentage of problems do 5 users find?
What SUS score do ten answers of 3 give?
flashcards.back: Each item contributes 2, so 20 × 2.5 = 50.

flashcards.front: Why does the 'five users' advice not mean that five users are a whole study?
flashcards.back: Five users find most problems in one round for one group, and the plan is to fix them and test again, since fixes and other groups reveal more.

flashcards.front: What value must |z| exceed for a result to be significant at the 95% level?
flashcards.back: At the 95% level the cut-off is 1.96 for a two-sided test.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the 95% level the cut-off is 1.96 for a two-sided test.

flashcards.front: Analytics show what users did and not the reason. The gap that needs qualitative research is the ____ gap.
flashcards.back: This is the why gap: counts locate a problem, and watching or asking people explains it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Counts locate a problem, and watching or asking people explains it.

flashcards.front: Why is stopping an A/B test the moment the result looks good a mistake?
flashcards.back: Each look at the data is another chance for chance to cross the threshold, so stopping early inflates false positives, and the sample size should be set in advance.

flashcards.front: How many heuristics are in Nielsen's list?
flashcards.back: The list has ten heuristics, from visibility of system status to help and documentation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The list has ten heuristics, from visibility of system status to help and documentation.

flashcards.front: Heuristic 1 asks the system to keep users informed. It is called visibility of system ____.
flashcards.back: Visibility of system status means feedback within a reasonable time, which lets users know what the system is doing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Feedback within a reasonable time lets users know what the system is doing.

flashcards.front: Why are the heuristics rules of thumb and not laws?
flashcards.back: They were derived from patterns in found problems and prompt questions about a design, and a problem can break several, so the evaluator judges which explains the most.

flashcards.front: Each evaluator finds 35% independently. What percentage do 3 find together, to one decimal place?
A walkthrough steps through a task asking four questions at each action, and is called a cognitive ____.
flashcards.back: In a cognitive walkthrough the questions are whether the user will try the effect, notice the action, connect it to the goal and see progress.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The questions are whether the user will try the effect, notice the action, connect it to the goal and see progress.

flashcards.front: Why should evaluators inspect independently before merging?
flashcards.back: Each finds a different part of the problems, and agreement beforehand would hide that and lower the total found.

flashcards.front: How many parts does a good error message have: what happened, why, and what to do next?
flashcards.back: The message should have these three parts, in the user's words, beside the field concerned.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The message should have these three parts, in the user's words, beside the field concerned.

flashcards.front: Reversing an action is usually better than asking 'Are you sure?', because people answer that by habit. The reversal is called ____.
flashcards.back: Undo costs nothing when the action was intended, and it is the better choice for reversible actions.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Undo costs nothing when the action was intended, and it is the better choice for reversible actions.

flashcards.front: Why is hint text inside a field not a replacement for a label?
flashcards.back: An in-field hint disappears when the user types and may not be announced as a name, so the field loses its name just when the user needs it.

flashcards.front: The four WCAG principles spell POUR. The O stands for ____.
flashcards.back: Operable means interface components and navigation must be usable, starting with the keyboard.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Operable means interface components and navigation must be usable, starting with the keyboard.

flashcards.front: What is the contrast ratio of black on white?
flashcards.back: (1 + 0.05) / (0 + 0.05) = 21, the largest possible.

flashcards.front: Why does #777777 text on white fail WCAG AA when #767676 passes?
flashcards.back: The ratios are 4.48 and 4.54, and 4.5 is the line for normal text, which is applied without rounding.

flashcards.front: What is the minimum pointer target size in CSS px under 2.5.8 (AA)?
flashcards.back: The target must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels unless an exception applies.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The target must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels unless an exception applies.

flashcards.front: A control that performs an action on the page should be a native ____ element.
flashcards.back: A button comes with focus, a role and keyboard activation without extra code.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A button comes with focus, a role and keyboard activation without extra code.

flashcards.front: Why should a decorative image have an empty alt and not no alt?
flashcards.back: An empty alt tells a screen reader to skip the image, and a missing alt can make it read the file name aloud.
